#1047. Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion

Felix Nmecha's "Crowns down" celebration has drawn criticism from a Borussia Dortmund fan club, reopening debate over faith, inclusion and religious messaging in football.

Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

"Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.

"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent."

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club said "gives us cause to reassess the situation."

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (BIG) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.

Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:

"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

"My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold."

Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.

The fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends."

Here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's plan" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone."

Article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

The use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit."

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the new opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.

With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

With around 10 minutes remaining in north London, you can follow our updates of that match here.

Erling Haaland will be hoping for his 10th league goal in 10 games this term, having bagged nine from nine so far.

Last week’s 1-0 defeat against Brighton was the first league game he failed to score in since the opening match of the season against Bournemouth.

The Norwegian is once again leading the way in the Premier League’s scoring charts, with three goals more than his nearest rivals.

Oliver Glasner pressed the nuclear button last weekend and the big question today is how his Forest players respond.

After the 2-0 defeat at Brentford, Glasner warned there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

This usually goes one of two ways and Glasner will be hoping it produces a positive reaction.

"If they don't want to follow, I guess the sixth manager will come in." Oliver Glasner is ready to make some changes at Nottingham Forest. https://t.co/xiCCA25IV4

Training has apparently been excellent this week but it will mean little unless they transfer it into a match situation.

James McAtee has been Forest’s best player so far this season and faces the club he joined as an 11 year old.

Enzo Maresca made a flawless start at Manchester City but is now enduring a stumble.

Two successive Premier League defeats have seen City replaced at the summit by Arsenal, so the importance of this match has gone up a notch.

Elliot Anderson returns for the first time since his £116m move from Forest in the summer and what a signing he already appears.

Forest are already wondering whether their asking price should have been higher and, as daft as it sounds, City have probably got a bargain.

There will be a lot of focus today on goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has been unconvincing in recent weeks.

Gianluigi Donnarumma with a huge mistake as Ridle Baku's near-post effort goes straight in 😬 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/r2K0C5jbqm

Maresca has made three changes following City’s 3-2 win at Leipzig in midweek, with Dias, Gvardiol and Doku replacing Nunes, O’Reilly and Foden.

Our line-up to face Forest! 👊🩵 XI | Donnarumma, Khusanov, Dias (C), Guéhi, Gvardiol, Anderson, Fernández, Ndiaye, Cherki, Doku, Haaland SUBS | Rulli, Kovačić, Reis, Nunes, Bouaddi, O'Reilly, Allan, Foden, Lewis 🤝 @etihad https://t.co/1N9iOorlpb

Glasner has made two changes to his Forest team following defeat at Brentford last weekend, with Yates and Munoz replacing Ndoye and Aina.

Is this the day the xG gods reward Nottingham Forest? Oliver Glasner’s team sit 19th having won one game all season, but there is no doubt that their performances have been significantly better than results and they might need their luck to turn against Man City team full of firepower.

Despite all of the positive indicators in Forest’s underlying data, Glasner caused some alarm with his comments after last weekend’s defeat at Brentford.

The Austrian said: “We have to accept it’s not good enough. If we lose four of the last five games, it’s not good enough. And that’s why for me, it’s now time that we change things, that I change things, and that’s what I will do.

“I feel now maybe I made too many compromises in some stuff, and it’s always compromises. It’s a clear way. I will tell [the players] what we want to do, what we have to do, and if the players buy in, I think we can have a turnaround, and if not, the sixth manager [since the start of last season] will come in.”

Dangerous words perhaps when you work for Evangelos Marinakis, but John Percy reported this week that Glasner was backed by his players in a squad meeting.

City are smarting from back-to-back defeats by Aston Villa and Brighton, but they created more than enough in both games to claim some sort of result. Nevertheless, there is a persistent sense that their defensive unit remains too marshmellow-like over the course of 38 games, and Forest have the counter-attacking threat to test them.

Glasner has happy memories of playing City, beating them in the 2025 FA Cup final with Crystal Palace, but his Forest reign is in urgent need of a signature victory and performance.

#1045. Mitre bring back iconic Ultimax ball to celebrate 30th anniversary

First launched in 1995, Mitreâs Ultimax ball quickly became a defining symbol in English football. A fixture on Premier League pitches throughout the 1990s, it made history as the first football to break the 100mph speed barrier.

Now, 30 years later, Mitre has reimagined the legendary ball, bringing it back with a modern twist.

The new Ultimax Pro 30th Anniversary Ball merges the classic design with cutting-edge technology, celebrating its iconic status while setting a new standard for the next generation.

While the ball retains the familiar 6-panel construction, the classic white, blue, and red colourway, and the unmistakable crown logo, itâs been upgraded with advanced features. Hyperflow grooves reduce drag and a sleek pearl finish offers a nod to traditional 30th-anniversary gifts. The interior also sees improvements, with Hyperfoam cushioning now enhanced for cleaner strikes and even more power.

To mark the milestone, Mitre has launched the "The Next In Line" campaign, spotlighting the new wave of football talent carrying on their family legacies.

The campaign features rising stars such as Raphaella Wright-Phillips, granddaughter of Arsenal icon Ian Wright, Ruben Butt, son of Manchester United legend Nicky Butt, and Jacob Fowler, whose father is Liverpoolâs own Robbie Fowler.

The trio, each in vintage 95/96 kits, embody the connection between the past and the future â just as the new Ultimax Pro does itself.

#1043. Newcastle host 'Road to Wembley' exhibition celebrating Carabao Cup triumph

Newcastle Unitedâs long wait for domestic silverware finally ended last season when they lifted the Carabao Cup â and the club marked the historic moment with a one-of-a-kind exhibition that captured the spirit of their journey to glory.

'The Road to Wembley', hosted at the Baltic Centre for Contemporary Art in collaboration with VERSUS, offered supporters an immersive, documentary-style retelling of the Magpiesâ cup success.

The exhibition featured more than 100 photographs by club photographers Serena Taylor, Harriet Massey and Michelle Mercer, each capturing intimate moments from the campaign. Visitors also experienced cinematic displays, installations from fan group Wor Flags, and the rare chance to stand alongside the Carabao Cup trophy itself.

The launch event included a panel featuring curators Ewen Spencer and Jimmy Turrell, alongside Newcastle legend Rob Lee, before celebrations spilled into the night with a DJ set.

The centrepiece of the story, of course, was Newcastleâs 2-1 victory over Liverpool in the final â sealed by Alexander Isakâs decisive strike.

With the Swede now not-so-subtly pining for a move to Liverpool, no less, the exhibition may have accidentally doubled up as his own farewell tour â a reminder that even if heroes donât always stick around, the memories (and the trophy) are here to stay.

#1042. An enduring climatic burden from past peatland drainage

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Over millennia, peatlands have removed hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere but emitted a proportion back as methane (CH4), exerting a slow net cooling effect1. Artificial drainage of these ecosystems—a centuries-old practice2,3—causes decomposition and the re-release of CO2 but suppresses CH4 emissions4, with a net climatic effect that is not well quantified at the global scale5. Here we reconstructed the radiative forcing from worldwide peatland drainage over 1800–2020 by combining a new flux dataset, hydrologically driven models of CO2 and CH4 fluxes and a hindcast of drainage extent and intensity. We found that drainage has produced a net heating effect of +73 (48–99) mW m−2—equivalent to 2.7 (1.8–3.6)% of industrial-era radiative forcing—originating from 0.4–0.5% of global land area. The net heating results from the dominant forcing of drainage-induced CO2 emissions (+83 (52–110) mW m−2) over that of avoided CH4 emissions (−9 (−15–−2) mW m−2). Even without further expansion of drainage, maintaining currently drained areas could almost double the cumulative warming by 2100. Our reconstruction captures the opposing impacts of peatland drainage on global budgets of CO2 and CH4 and quantifies the strong legacy effects of historical drainage on present and possibly future climate.

#1039. Megaspeed and the battle to go high-end Nvidia chips into China

Jensen Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy has shone a light on Megaspeed, the company she worked for. It is under investigation in the US for smuggling Nvidia chips into China, which it denies.

As Nvidia, one of the world's most valuable companies, grapples with CEO Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, attention is turning to the much smaller company she worked for.

Alice H., the alleged spy, worked as an executive for Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center and AI computing company. It manages data center access, including for some major Chinese tech firms such as Alibaba.

According to Megaspeed's website as of November 2026, the company advertises itself as an "Nvidia cloud partner", saying it provides "computing power product services covering Nvidia's entire GPU product line." GPU stands for Graphic Processing Unit, a specialized electronic circuit that are in high demand for artificial intelligence (AI) applications, because they are designed to handle high numbers of parallel mathematical calculations. Megaspeed says it provides access for clients to Nvidia's advanced GB200 NVL72 ​computing system.

This type of firm is often referred to as a "neocloud". It buys Nvidia chips and computing power and then rents it out — in this case, at multiple sites across south-east Asia, to different companies. The US has set up strict export controls to prevent that Nvidia's high-performance chips end up in China, because it sees China as a competitor in the global AI race. It also does not want data centers made up of Nvidia chips to be owned by Chinese companies. It does, however, tolerate that data center compute with Nvidia chips be rented out to Chinese companies like Alibaba, and occasionally allows the export of Nvidia chips for specific purposes.

Megaspeed has bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia's products in recent years and has been accused of breaching US export controls to divert Nvidia chips into China.

In December 2025, Bloomberg reported that the "once-obscure" Megaspeed had become the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in all of south-east Asia and that the US government was investigating its ownership structure and whether or not it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China.

At the same time, Singapore police began an investigation into whether or not Megaspeed had "violated local laws" without specifying which ones. Those investigations are believed to be still ongoing.

On December 23, 2025, Megaspeed strenuously denied any wrongdoing in a statement — which still appears as the first page for visitors to the company's website as of November 2026.

"There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company," it said. "We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct."

The US government investigation began in 2024. The Commerce Department initially began looking into Megaspeed, but the US Justice Department has since taken over. According to the New York Times, this switch came about after an Nvidia executive directly contacted the Commerce Department about the investigation.

Megaspeed was founded in 2015 and was originally called 7Road International. It changed its name to Megaspeed in March 2023. It is owned by the Singapore-registered Swiftdata, which was set up in October 2023.

Its rise in prominence coincided with a sharp increase in assets, which increased from $33 million in 2023 to $3 billion in 2024.

Alice H., the woman accused of being a Chinese spy, had an affair with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. She is widely seen as an influential figurehead at Megaspeed. She also served as the company's managing director of Megaspeed for eight months in 2023.

The Financial Times reported on Monday that Alice H. leveraged her close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia to pitch AI chips deals to Chinese investors.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The newspaper said that in early 2025, Alice H. sought investment in China for a data center project in south-east Asia, and cited their easy access to Nvidia chips and close relationship with Alibaba.

Alibaba lent money to Megaspeed in June 2024, via subsidiaries. It has remained Megaspeed's largest client, according to reporting by the Financial Times.

In December 2025, Nvidia said its own inquiry into Megaspeed had found no evidence of chips being diverted and that the company was fully owned and operated outside of China, with no Chinese shareholders. The company told Bloomberg at the time that it had visited Megaspeed's facilities on multiple occasions and had seen nothing untoward.

Megaspeed is one of several companies accused of smuggling Nvidia's chips into China or finding ways to give Chinese companies access to them.

Nvidia's high-performance chips are seen as essential for companies looking for the most advanced form of supercomputing to use and develop various AI applications.

Back in 2022, the Biden Administration began severely restricting the sale of the US's most advanced chips to China, part of the two countries' growing rivalry to achieve AI dominance.

However, an illegal smuggling and underground network was soon set up, with many vendors operating to get the chips into China and selling them on to companies there.

In December 2025, US authorities shut down the operations of Hao Global, a US-based shell company with links to China which plead guilty to smuggling Nvidia chips to China.

In June 2026, Taiwanese government agencies raided the offices of Super Micro Computer as part of an investigation into the smuggling of Nvidia chips to China.

While export restrictions have been eased significantly under the Trump administration, there are still significant blocks and restrictions on the most advanced Nvidia chips.

In December 2025, the Trump administration approved several Chinese companies to buy or handle advanced Nvidia H200 chips, a move that sparked significant concern among the US security establishment.

However, that deal has not led to a significant flow of Nvidia chips moving legally to China, amid strict US licencing controls and official reluctance from Beijing to publicly promote Nvidia chips to the detriment of its own alternatives.

Emile Heskey is standing in a warehouse, dressed in a black adidas tracksuit, trying to sell you a jar of curious sweet treats.

Behind him, stacked on shelf after shelf, are containers full of Supreme CBD gummies.

The man who scored in England's 5-1 thrashing of Germany in 2001, who scored 110 Premier League goals for Leicester, Liverpool, Birmingham, Wigan and Aston Villa plus seven more for his country, is, remarkably, trying to flog you an assortment of products containing cannabidiol, a legal but controversial ingredient derived from cannabis.

Today, he is promoting a tub of CBD strawberry gummies, as well as oil. If you fancy an exclusive discount, there's a special code bearing his name.

‘I swear by these products for my sleep,’ he writes in the caption on Instagram. ‘They have been fantastic for me for years now!’

Heskey, 48, was once one of English football's most respected players. He won 62 caps for England, appearing at two World Cups. He won five trophies at Liverpool and two League Cups at Leicester.

Occasionally mocked for his lack of goals – he averaged roughly one every five games during his club career – he carried himself with humour and grace. Since retiring, his reputation has helped him secure roles with England's youth pathway and Leicester's women's team, as well as occasional punditry work for the BBC.

In September, he scored in an England legends match against Poland, playing alongside John Terry and Robbie Fowler. This month, he was a guest of honour at Liverpool's Anfield VIP Experience. He remains a regular on the speakers' circuit, with more appearances booked before Christmas.

All of which begs the question: what is he doing promoting Supreme CBD? Why is he filming several videos a month for a company with such a troubled regulatory record?

Where once he shared a dressing room with Steven Gerrard and David Beckham, he now shares an ambassadorial roster with Katie Price.

It is unclear whether Heskey is aware of the concerns surrounding Supreme CBD products, or the repeated occasions on which the company has fallen foul of advertising rules.

Its founder, Anthony Fowler, a former Team GB Olympic boxer, has made unsubstantiated claims that his cannabidiol products can help treat mental health conditions and autism in children.

There is likely a financial incentive for Heskey, although the terms of any arrangement are unclear. Equally, he appears genuinely convinced of the products' benefits. He claims the oil has done wonders for his sleep and eased his aches and pains.

That may well be true. The NHS acknowledges that CBD has some medical uses, but warns that the ‘quality and content’ of products sold online can be uncertain and that they ‘may be illegal and potentially dangerous’. Nor is there any guarantee that products sold in health stores will be of ‘good quality’.

Supreme CBD have repeatedly breached advertising rules. In June, the Advertising Standards Authority took action over the company's continued use of prohibited claims that CBD could treat, prevent or cure human disease.

The regulator has also upheld complaints about celebrity promotions that failed to make clear they were advertisements.

Supreme CBD have made claims that their products can treat anxiety, insomnia and depression. Such medicinal claims are prohibited in advertising for products that have not been authorised as medicines. It is uncomfortable ground for Heskey to find himself on.

Last year, Fowler also spoke about refusing chemotherapy for his two-year-old daughter's tumour, claiming CBD oil had had a 'massive' effect on it instead. Price, a paid brand ambassador, amplified those claims on her own social media channels, including posted to her 1.6million followers on X that the tumour had 'shrunk' as a result.

British medical and food safety authorities advise that CBD should not be given to those under the age of 18.

CBD can also affect how other medicines work, meaning anyone using it alongside other treatments should seek medical advice. Certain medicinal CBD treatments require regular monitoring because of their potential effects on the liver.

It is not unusual for former sportspeople to struggle with insomnia, depression or persistent pain after retirement. In a digital world where anyone can extol the virtues of a product to thousands of followers, it is perhaps unsurprising that cannabis oil has attracted so much attention. #1030. Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?

Hitler once called Eastern Europe "Germany's India." A new exhibition examines the links between colonialism and Nazism, and the bitter debate over where comparisons illuminate history and where they fall short.

Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men."

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared remains the subject of intense debate.

This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

"I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposedly be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.

The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust.

Yet it also points to connections: Whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

In the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing new or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people."

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

The Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met.

Forced labor was also central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.

While racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski says the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities, for example at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," says Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued."

On October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic. Even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.

The issue of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

Since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

The mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. But in 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.

Martinican intellectual Aime Cesaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. More than 70 years later, the exhibition opens amid renewed debates over the definition of settler colonialism and genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over Germany's support for Israel during the war in Gaza and its alleged failure to uphold its obligations under the Genocide Convention to prevent genocide.

These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

Germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance.  However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy.

"I think Germans and all other human beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi said. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027.

#1026. Just eight universities dominate Nobel and other top economics prizes

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Sarah Wild is a freelance journalist in Canterbury, UK.

Researchers from Harvard and seven other US universities including MIT, Princeton and Yale, dominate economics prizes.Credit: Jade Gao/AFP via Getty

Major prizes in economics, including the Nobel are being awarded to researchers affiliated to an increasingly concentrated set of US universities, according to a working paper published last month1.

Eight institutions dominate the world's top economics prizes, led Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts.

This contrasts with prizes awarded in disciplines in the natural sciences, engineering and social sciences outside economics. These have become less concentrated among certain instituions over the past 70 years, according to the working paper, which has not yet been peer reviewed.

“The whole world now does science,” says Richard Freeman, an economist at Harvard University and an author on the paper, which is an update to an article presented at a National Bureau of Economic Research Summer Institute workshop in a 20242. “Our initial thought was that as the science spreads out, so too should all the prizes.” And that was the case — except in economics where “it went the other direction”.

Economist John Hassler, who is based at Stockholm University and chairs the prize-awarding committee for the Economics Prize in Memory of Alfred Nobel, says that the overall finding of concentration among a small group of US universities is not a complete surprise.

“The trend is truly eye-opening and adds another dimension to the understanding of inequality within the economics profession,” adds Ashwini Deshpande, an economist at Ashoka University in Sonipat, India. “The low levels of gender, ethnic and geographic diversity within authors of top journal papers and prizes is well known and a matter of concern.”

Freeman and his colleagues examined 171 different awards and focused their analyses on those given between 1960 and 2022, including Nobel prizes (except for literature and peace), the Fields Medal for mathematics and the Breakthrough science prizes established in 2012 by the founders of technology companies among others.

The authors of the working paper analysed the academic affiliations of the 5,859 prizewinners, working out the number of years they were linked to a specific institution. They call this metric ‘affiliation years’.

Of the 18 scientific fields of the prizewinners, 17 had a greater variety of universities represented among recipients over the time period. Economics was the outlier.

Among winners of the economics Nobel prize, seven out of 148 institutions made up 50% of affiliation years. It means that, of all the years that economics Nobel prizewinners dedicated to their discipline in academia, half of them were spent in the seven institutions.

For chemistry Nobels, 23 institutions out of 216 accounted for half of affiliation years. Twenty-six out of 243 institutions accounted for 50% of affiliation years for the physiology or medicine Nobel, and 17 out of 200 for the physics prize.

When the authors assessed all the main economics prizes between 1960 and 2022 (not only the Nobel), they found that researchers from eight out of 249 institutions represented 50% of affiliation years. In addition to Harvard, the eight are: the University of Chicago in Illinois; Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge; Stanford University in California; Princeton University in New Jersey; Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut; the University of California, Berkeley; and Columbia University in New York.

By contrast, for assessed prizes in the natural sciences, 37 institutions out of 1,318 account for 50% of affiliation-years as of 2022; for engineering prizes it is 27 out of 783; and for social sciences prizes (minus economics), it is 23 out of 744. Unlike in economics, the trend for these fields is towards less concentration (see ‘Spot the outlier’).

The authors propose some possible explanations. One of these relates to another finding of the paper: “The institutions producing most of the field’s recognized work also establish the toolkit that the rest of the fields adopts,” the paper’s authors say. “Work using an unfamiliar approach is hard to place or recognize, and findings that disagree with the main tenets of the field are rejected rather than studied as special cases that may yield new knowledge.”

Another factor, they report is that in economics, 55 per cent of Nobel laureates received the prize for a broad body of work. This contrasts somewhat with medicine and the other sciences. Some 50 per cent of prize winners in chemistry, 59 per cent in physics and 70 per cent in medicine were awarded for testable findings.

Hanzhang Zhou, a co-author on the paper and an economics doctoral candidate at MIT, says: “When you’re giving the prize for somebody’s lifetime agenda, the institution that they’re associated with is usually one of the factors that you do take into account,” she explains.

Hassler told Nature that the economics prize is not intended to be a lifetime achievement award and follows the rules governing the other prize categories. He says it is a prize for a well-defined contribution or breakthrough, should also lead to further research in the field and that the finding must also have relevance to society at large.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03333-3

Freeman, R. B., Xie, D., Zhang, H. & Zhou, H. NBER Working Paper 35875 (National Bureau of Economic Research, 2026).

Freeman, R. B., Xie, D., Zhang, H. & Zhou, H. in NBER Summer Institute – The Science of Science Funding https://conference.nber.org/conf_papers/f204525.pdf (2024).

#1025. How Man United's data gurus got Leny Yoro off the hook: Stats analysis from ex-Formula One boffin proved Alexander Isak had NO chance of reaching the ball before red card - in appeal win that has left refs fuming

Published: 07:49 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 11:31 EST, 26 November 2026

Manchester United turned to its data gurus in a bid to categorically prove Alexander Isak had no chance of reaching the ball as part of its evidence to overturn Leny Yoro’s red card.

Yoro was sent off eight minutes into United’s trip to Anfield for a last-man foul on Isak, which referee Sam Barrott determined fit the criteria for Denial Of A Goalscoring Opportunity (DOGSO).

The young United centre-back was shown a straight red card after VAR doubled down on the day, insisting that no ‘clear and obvious error’ had been made.

United successfully appealed the decision through an independent panel and the lengths they went to for their evidence submission has now come to light.

Bosses at United included three high-definition video clips of the incident in question, which used multiple different angles as well as speeds in slow-motion and in real time for the panel to consider.

United also submitted video evidence of a DOGSO sending off earlier this season for Brighton’s Pascal Struijk against Sunderland, which was also overturned on appeal.

Leny Yoro was sent off for Man United against Liverpool but the red card was later rescinded

United showed that Isak would not have reached the ball if he'd have stayed on his feet

The most fascinating element of United’s detailed evidence pack came via its data department, led by ex-Formula One guru Michael Sansoni.

United outlined in a letter to the appeal panel that a technical analysis of the incident saw boffins at Carrington calculate the probability of Isak reaching the ball following his heavy touch prior to contact from Yoro.

The data allowed for the possibility that Isak maintained his speed and direction from the moment his legs first made contact with Yoro to assess whether he would have got to the ball before United goalkeeper Senne Lammens.

United’s analysis concluded that Isak would have been 1.8 metres shy of reaching the ball even if all optimal speed and directional factors had been achieved.

The appeals commission, however, told United that that data, however detailed, was not verifiable and so had to be treated with ‘caution’.

Considering all the elements of United’s submission, the panel unanimously agreed that it was not a red card offence and did not meet the threshold for DOGSO, immediately overturning the decision and withdrawing all punishment against Yoro.

‘We can accept referee can make a mistake. But we have VAR. What were they doing?’ a fuming Mauricio Pochettino said on Tuesday of the original Yoro decision.

‘We are going to repeat the game? Play similar tools the game XI v XI? We have an unbelievable car but we have to be at the level to drive. We accept the technology.’

#1024. Germany slips in climate protection rankings as other countries make gains

Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

Germany has slipped down the climate action ranking for the third consecutive year, with the former green leader now being outperformed by Brazil, Colombia and Romania.

In its worst performance since 2019, the country fell to place 25 and received a "medium" rating overall on the yearly Climate Change Performance Index (CCPI), which assesses efforts to curb global warming in 64 countries plus the European Union.

Still, "a number of countries have been making good progress for years," said Jan Burck, CCPI lead author, in a statement. Denmark is leading the way across all four categories assessed — energy use, greenhouse gas emissions, renewable energy and national climate policy. A total of 15 states, including Lithuania, Chile, and Morocco, received an overall "high" rating, which is two more than last year.

The European Union also moved up a spot, while Hungary jumped 21 places after the ousting of former prime minister Viktor Orban's government, which had repeatedly vetoed EU climate plans, dismissing them as a "utopian fantasy."

The top three positions on the CCPI remained vacant again this year, as no country has yet done enough to meet global climate goals aimed at preventing worsening weather extremes and climate damage.

"We are seeing a striking contrast," said Burck. "Progress on climate action is often slow and in some countries, such as the United States, things are even moving backwards. But technologically and economically there is enormous momentum."

That momentum is apparent in record solar energy growth. Last year 75% of global electricity demand growth was met by the green energy source, according to energy think tank Ember's latest global electricity review. Investment in clean energy has also outpaced that in fossil fuels for multiple years.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The rapid expansion of renewable technology, as well as the Iran War and a reduction in deforestation are behind a projected slight fall in emissions for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to the CCPI.

"Governments have to act now to turn the momentum into sustained emissions reductions," said CCPI co-author Niklas Höhne of the NewClimate Institute, which compiles the report with environmental NGO Germanwatch.

Burck attributed Germany's worst ever performance in the category of national climate policy to current policies being pursued by Germany's economy minister Katherina Reiche.

"Measures that primarily aim to increase the use of natural gas, threaten to undermine progress in the energy transition and risk significantly worsening the conditions for renewable energy and electrification for many years to come," said Burck.

A European Commission report published on November 9 on the sidelines of the UN COP31 climate summit in Turkey said Germany was one of nine EU countries set to miss 2030 emissions reductions targets.

Germany is not alone in its disappointing ranking. The other G20 countries — the world's leading industrialized and emerging economies, responsible for around 80% of global CO2 emissions — also perform poorly.

The only exception among them is the United Kingdom, which ranks seventh and received a high rating, performing well in greenhouse gas emissions, energy use and climate policy. However, study authors rated it low for renewable energy expansion.

The G20's oil- and gas-producing countries occupy some of the lowest positions on the climate action table. The United States, which is the world's second largest emitter, languishes alongside Russia, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Canada around the bottom of the league, with an overall rating of "very low."

The hosts of this year's COP31, also received a "low" overall score. Australia, a major coal exporter with some of the world's highest per-capita emissions, ranks 54th, while Turkey, which is also heavily dependent on fossil fuels, comes in 53rd.

China is the world's largest emitter of greenhouse gases and ranks 56th in the CCPI, receiving an overall rating of "very low." Its main weaknesses include its now high per-capita emissions and substantial energy consumption.

However, among the G20, China leads the way in renewable energy expansion. The country, which is five years ahead of schedule in reaching its goal of adding 1,200 GW of wind and solar capacity to the grid by 2030, also produces over 80% of the world's solar panels.

Several oil-producing countries, including Kazakhstan, Saudi Arabia, Uzbekistan and the United Arab Emirates, are also performing better than expected in the renewables category and "are significantly expanding their previously limited" capacity, said the report.

The authors said these countries have significant potential to further expand renewables.

"In the Arab states in particular, very high per-capita emissions and an above-average level of electrification coincide with a relatively low existing share of renewable energy and enormous solar potential," said co-author Natalie Pelekh in a statement. "These are, in fact, ideal conditions for more ambitious climate action."

This article was originally published in German.

A mostly compact performance out of possession briefly became as porous as a bath sponge when Liverpool eased into a 2-0 lead, nine minutes after half-time. Florian Wirtz did not even need to finish cleanly to score his first Premier League goal of the season, striding on to an unopposed low cross from Bradley Barcola and killing the match as a contest.

Neither left Selhurst Park looking like the world-beaters they did occasionally for their previous clubs. Liverpool are popping the ball around with real intent as Gakpo clips a teasing cross into Barcola. It’s just out of the winger’s reach, with Barcola claiming he was pushed by Mingueza. Liverpool then win a free kick after Mingueza blocks Kerkez’s run, but Mac Allister glances Szoboszlai’s cross into the side netting at the near post.

Fun start. Palace have occasionally looked like they are hanging on for dear life when defending, especially whenever Gakpo has been on the ball, but have looked capable of some attacking threat of their own, through Pino and Timber especially. Barcola the first example of a player obeying Iraola’s advice to go down more, collapsing from a gentle push after climbing for a header he was never like to reach. Gets short shrift from the referee and Palace fans.

It’s been a fast-paced and frantic start to this game. Isak’s delightful touch takes him away from Disasi, who pulls the Liverpool forward to the ground, giving the visitors a free kick. The Palace defender is perhaps lucky to avoid a yellow card for that foul.

Mitchell lashes a dangerous delivery across the six-yard box towards Strand Larsen, but solid defensive work from Van Dijk and Araujo allow Liverpool to clear.

Barcola lofts a ball over the top of Palace’s backline for Isak to latch onto. However, Disasi recovers well and blocks the Liverpool striker’s fierce half-volley from a tight angle.

A loose pass at the back from Palace gifts Liverpool an early opportunity, but Henderson does well to get down low and gather Mac Allister’s low, fizzing effort from outside the penalty area.

Liverpool get us under way at Selhurst Park. Can Iraola inflict more misery on Sage?

A pretty meek rendition of Glad All Over greets the players as they come out of the tunnel, althoiugh it is hardly the sort of rabble-rousing song to strike fear into an opponent at the best of times. #1018. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

You know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a new task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

It turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

But it's important to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

There's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?"

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice important signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

Maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great new idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

Scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

Take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

You can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

#1013. ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Mathematics Álvaro Lozano-Robledo thought the Riemann hypothesis was out of AI’s reach for now.Credit: Bri Diaz/UConn Photo

The news came on a Friday — and it was ground-shaking. For months, reports have mounted of artificial-intelligence models toppling some of the toughest problems in mathematics, plunging the field into turmoil. But the latest claim was the most shocking yet: an AI model had helped to solve the field’s most famous open problem, the Riemann hypothesis.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The proof was released on 20 November by mathematician Levent Alpöge at AI giant Anthropic in San Francisco, California, who used an advanced version of the firm’s Claude model. It came in the form of 17 million lines of code in the open-source programming language Lean, which translates mathematical arguments into computer-certifiable code. In a matter of hours, a separate set of mathematicians rushed out a human-written proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which is in the branch of number theory and pertains to the randomness of prime numbers.

Alpöge’s proof has been independently verified by the non-profit organization behind Lean and the Mathlib Initiative, which runs the reference library of formalized mathematics results written in Lean. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him,” the community said in a statement on 21 November.

The mathematics community has broadly accepted the claim, although responses differ wildly. Some celebrate Alpöge’s achievement, but others see the development as proof that humans are fighting against machines for the future of mathematics.

Nature hears reactions from five mathematicians on what solving the Riemann hypothesis means to them.

Mathematician Tasmin Chu is part of the Association for Human Mathematics, whose members commit to doing AI-free research.Credit: Elizabeth Xiao

Tasmin Chu, PhD student in mathematics at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena.

A technology that can autonomously prove the Riemann hypothesis is no trivial matter. I think that it is imperative our society acts to pause AI development as soon as possible. Over the past year, mathematical institutions have faced the impossible task of adapting to the rapidly changing capabilities of AI in real time.

It’s enormously disruptive for early-career researchers — the people who are the intellectual future of our field. Soon other sectors of society will face the same issues.

My reaction is grave concern. AI companies urgently require democratic oversight. I do not think AI’s encroachment into math is inevitable, nor is the death of human mathematical practice inevitable. It’s a choice to disempower ourselves, just as it’s a choice to continue building these technologies despite grave safety concerns. I continue to practice mathematics without LLMs, because I believe it’s critical that scientific inquiry continues in the hands of human beings. Some of us at the Association for Human Mathematics — whose organizing committee I am on — are collectively making the same decision.

Harini Desiraju, lecturer in mathematics at the University of Warwick, UK.

Given the events of the past few months, this news wasn't entirely a surprise, but we need to wait to understand the Lean proof and let the experts verify it. It is several million lines of code, after all.

I am not a number theorist, so I might not have the same emotional attachment to the Riemann hypothesis. Nevertheless, I have deep appreciation for the ubiquity and the importance of the problem in several areas of maths and physics.

As for the recent events, I want to distinguish between formal proofs versus knowledge. It is an impressive feat to solve such a problem. However, because it is a Lean proof over millions of lines, it is going to take a while before the community gets real understanding, and validity of the proof. With an AI-independent approach available as well, it could present a great opportunity for discovery of new ideas and mathematics. We need to see how it all plays out.

There is another discussion to be had, which involves the role of frontier labs in research. Most of us see the potential benefits of this technology, but it is of utmost importance that we work towards a future where the agency is with the scientific community and not a couple of companies.

Mathematician Marcus Du Sautoy is anxious about what’s next for his field.Credit: David Levenson/Getty

Marcus Du Sautoy, mathematician and professor for the public understanding of science at the University of Oxford, UK.

It was real mix of emotions. A part of me says, how exciting to be alive when this great problem was solved! I think even when Fermat’s last theorem was solved, we had the same excitement and the same melancholy: that great motivator is gone.

Mixed in with that, is the complete surprise that it ended up being proved this way. If you’d asked me three months ago, I would never have predicted it.

There’s quite a lot of anxiety about what ‘math 2.0’ is going to look like.

Xin Zhang, assistant professor in mathematics at the University of Hong Kong.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03835-0

Nottingham Forest's restless players have already seen off two managers in the past 12 months but now Oliver Glasner believes he will beat them at their own game.

The strength of feeling within the squad helped force Ange Postecoglou and Sean Dyche out of the door after 39 and 114 days respectively and after a dodgy start to his reign, there were probably one or two who thought Glasner would go the same way.

No Premier League boss is ever immune to results and another run of defeats would make Glasner vulnerable. Forest have won two games all season and are above the relegation zone only on goal difference, ahead of Friday night’s clash with Chelsea at the City Ground.

But as things stand, Glasner has the backing of Forest owner Evangelos Marinakis to make the changes he needs – and that could be bad news for some senior players.

Daily Mail Sport examines the power struggle bubbling away at the City Ground...

Nottingham Forest's restless players have already seen off two managers in the past 12 months but now Oliver Glasner believes he will beat them at their own game

Glasner took aim at some players' lack of English skills in light of a disappointing start to the season that sees his side hovering outside the relegation zone on goal difference alone

Early in his reign, Mikel Arteta stamped his authority on Arsenal, moving on high-profile players like Mesut Ozil, Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang and Alexandre Lacazette.

Even at the start of his managerial career, Arteta would not compromise and was prepared to clash with big names if they would not match his standards. Arteta knew what he wanted and if he had to fight some stars to get it, all well and good. Now look where Arsenal are today.

It will not have escaped Glasner that despite their success, the champions work ferociously hard and seem to carry no outsized egos or sense of entitlement. That may worry certain Forest players.

This is the source of Glasner’s remarks about players not learning English – but that is not his only issue with the squad. He wants time-keeping to be sharper, training sessions to be slicker.

It is thought Forest will listen to offers for Ola Aina and Callum Hudson-Odoi in January, while Ibrahim Sangare has work to do to force his way into Glasner’s plans. Hudson-Odoi and Aina are influential figures in the dressing room and Sangare is highly respected, too. Is Glasner trying to smash this power base in order to cement his own?

Glasner wants to add more athleticism and physicality to his squad in January as he has been alarmed at how Forest have been outmuscled in certain games. As things stand, he has the mandate to shape things his way after a three-hour meeting with Marinakis in London this week.

It will not be easy. Glasner can change some things yet a fair number of this squad are on their fifth manager. They were outstanding for a season under Nuno Espirito Santo in 2024-25 but they have drifted since. It still feels a long way until January and that is why – more than ever – Glasner needs the captain on board...

Glasner wants players' time-keeping to be sharper and training sessions to be slicker

It is thought Forest will listen to offers for influential full back Ola Aina in January

A glance at the numbers shows that Morgan Gibbs-White is having an outstanding season. He has created the second-most big chances of any player, the third-most chances from open play, and is in the top three for 'expected assists' too. Not bad for a player in a team above the relegation zone thanks only to goal difference.

Albeit from a smaller sample size, Gibbs-White is performing better than last term on all of these metrics (per 90 minutes). Last season, he finished with 15 league goals and four assists. England boss Thomas Tuchel appreciates the underlying numbers and after leaving Gibbs-White out of his World Cup squad, has brought him back into the fold this autumn.

Gibbs-White is Forest’s most talented player and it is believed he would have accepted a move away from the club last summer, after watching Elliot Anderson join Manchester City.

There was tentative interest from Chelsea but Gibbs-White wanted to play in the Champions League and it is thought he would have been open to a move to Manchester United. The 26-year-old’s boyhood idol was Wayne Rooney – but the Old Trafford club have never truly pushed for him. That may change if Bruno Fernandes leaves next summer.

Gibbs-White is the highest-paid player in Forest's history and is halfway through a three-year deal. Few expect him to be at the club for life and if he moves in summer 2027, nobody will be surprised.

Yet there is a feeling in the game that Gibbs-White’s body language can count against him at times. When team-mates are not quite on his wavelength, Gibbs-White is often quick to show his frustration. If he creates a chance that a colleague misses, it is a similar story.

Morgan Gibbs-White's numbers are very impressive this season. At times, the same can't be said for his body language

It is difficult to be rational in the heat of battle but could Gibbs-White try to stop these issues at source? At Forest, each part of the team – defenders, midfielders and forwards – have discussions before matches. That would be the perfect opportunity for Gibbs-White to guide others, to explain his thinking and where they should be when he has the ball in certain areas.

Because unless the player is Diego Maradona or Lionel Messi, top clubs do not look at talent alone before making signings. Gibbs-White has the tools to play for an elite team but in other aspects, there may still be some work to do.

Glasner and his staff hope Forest’s best player can inspire others, as he has in the past. Club skipper Ryan Yates returned to the starting XI for the last two matches and if he loses his place against Chelsea, Gibbs-White would logically regain the armband. How Forest need a captain’s performance from him against Xabi Alonso’s faltering side.

#1006. Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate?

World leaders warn that geopolitical divisions are distracting from the climate crisis as negotiations focus on clean energy and financing, while Iran calls for compensation for war-related environmental damage.

The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he said, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by New Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres said the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach."

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives are discussing climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, one of the few heads of government from Europe's major economies attending the summit, said that the world's dependence on fossil fuels was at the heart of both the climate crisis and energy security challenges.

"The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security," he said, endorsing the conference's focus on electrification which he said would lower energy bills, create jobs and protect people from the volatility of fossil fuel markets.

Burnham promised a "new era of British leadership over the next decade," announcing the UK would put climate resilience high on the agenda during its G20 presidency next year.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the summit — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including big polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

On Wednesday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

Financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

Erdogan said while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest."

"Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she said, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 2026.

Most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, said the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and quickly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over."

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," said Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

"We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Albanese said it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most."

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she said, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres said, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands said electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the issue to climate finance and said his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms."

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, said the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

He also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he said.

This article was last updated on November 12 to reflect incoming statements from world leaders.
