#963. Darren Bent's beach ball bedlam, Nani's controversial quick-thinking and Peter Enckelman's calamitous mishap: Our experts pick the strangest goals they have ever seen after Bruno Fernandes' 'divot strike' in Lisbon

Published: 15:03 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 15:03 EST, 26 November 2026

Bruno Fernandes and Manchester United were the beneficiaries of a bizarre goal in the Champions League on Wednesday night, as the captain's long-range effort bounced up off the turf and deceived the goalkeeper to help earn Mauricio Pochettino a 2-2 draw with Sporting Lisbon in his second game in charge.

Football has certainly seen its fair share of quirky, bizarre and downright bonkers goals over the years, and Fernandes' effort in Lisbon is certainly one to add to the collection.

Here, Daily Mail Sport's reporters look back at some of the strangest goals they can remember, from outrageous goalkeeping blunders to freakish deflections and moments of sheer misfortune.

Darren Bent (Sunderland 1-0 Liverpool) - October 17, 2009

Forget bouncing in off a divot, try the ball flying into the net off a beach ball. Darren Bent’s winner against Liverpool at the Stadium of Light back in 2009 has got to be the strangest.

A Liverpool fan lobbed a gigantic red beach ball on to the pitch (in the middle of October) which was initially removed by a steward only for the wind to blow it back.

What made it even funnier was that when Bent’s shot struck it, Liverpool keeper Pepe Reina tried to save the inflatable, which now resides in the National Football Museum, instead of the actual ball that flew past him.

Thank heavens there was no VAR back then to spoil the day.

Pepe Reina had no chance after Darren Bent's strike ricocheted off a beach ball into the goal

Peter Enckelman (Birmingham vs Aston Villa) - September 16, 2002

Obviously the mind immediately goes to balloons and players ghosting behind goalkeepers. But my favourite happened on September 16, 2002 between Birmingham City and Aston Villa.

Olof Mellberg took a throw-in. He threw it back to Peter Enckelman. The ball bounced under Enckelman’s foot and rolled into the Villa goal. Referee David Elleray reckoned he must have touched it with his studs.

It was all made worse for Enckelman with a Birmingham fan hopping out of the crowd to goad him to his face. I must have been nine years old and remember watching all this live.

Can’t imagine my parents told me what that hand gesture the fan was doing in front of Enckelman meant.

Peter Enckelman scored a disastrous own goal after the ball bounced underneath his foot

Mo Diame (Brighton vs Newcastle) - February 28, 2017

Brighton half cleared a corner and Christian Atsu returned a scuffed volley, which was helped on by the toe of Daryl Murphy, before Mo Diame planted his foot in the ground and allowed the ball to bounce off the back of his heel, looping up and over all inside the goalmouth and into the top corner.

I was there, and I have revisited my match report.

'Diame had been stood still for the majority of the previous 81 minutes,' I wrote. 'Finally, it was a tactic which served him well.'

I also refer to the goal as fluky and hilarious. It is now the stuff of legend on Tyneside, for it helped Newcastle to win promotion as champions. Indeed, without it, Brighton would have finished top and Newcastle second.

Mo Diame scored one of the craziest goals in Championship history against Brighton in 2017

Tony Popovic (Portsmouth vs Crystal Palace) - September 11, 2004

Some goals stay with you because of the sublime, others because of the ridiculous. And I doubt I'll ever see a stranger goal live than Tony Popovic's flying backheel into his own net in 2004.

With Portsmouth protecting a 2-1 lead late on against Crystal Palace, nerves were jangling around Fratton Park until Popovic's moment of spectacular misfortune.

Pompey's Steve Stone floated a hopeful cross into the Palace box, prompting Popovic to stretch out a leg in an attempt to clear. Instead, he somehow managed to flick the ball off his boot, onto the post and into the net, producing a finish any top striker would be proud of.

Portsmouth couldn't believe their luck when Tony Popovic flicked the ball into in his own net

Nani (Manchester United vs Tottenham) - October 30, 2010

This one has always stuck with me, partly for the sheer audacity of Nani and partly because it's the sort of goal that simply wouldn't escape VAR scrutiny today.

Back when a trip to Manchester United was still a fearsome prospect, Spurs were a goal down and chasing a late equaliser when Nani was brought down in the penalty area and appeared to handle the ball.

Crucially, though, Mark Clattenburg had not blown his whistle. Tottenham goalkeeper Heurelho Gomes, assuming a free-kick had been awarded, placed the ball on the ground.

Still gesticulating, Nani got up, realised the ball was still live, and coolly passed it into the back of the net. Cue bedlam in the Stretford End.

Nani celebrates his controversial goal against Spurs, to the fury of goalkeeper Heurelho Gomes

Zlatan Ibrahimovic (Sweden vs England) - November 14, 2012

It's not weird in the category of a divot or a beach ball but the most outlandish goal I've ever seen live was Zlatan Ibrahimovic's 30-yard overhead kick for Sweden against England at the Friends Arena in Stockholm in November 2012.

A long ball came over the top of the England defence, Joe Hart ran out and headed it clear and Ibrahimovic launched himself into the air, hooking the ball in a majestic arc over England's disbelieving goalkeeper. Great goals can be strange, too.

Zlatan Ibrahimovic's acrobatic bicycle kick against England was both strange and sensational

Stan Collymore (Blackburn vs Liverpool) - February 24, 1996

As soon as I watched Fernandes' speculative long-range strike bobble past Sporting Lisbon goalkeeper Kaique Pereira, my mind immediately cast back to Tim Flowers being embarrassed by Stan Collymore at Ewood Park in 1996.

Not that it was the Blackburn goalkeeper's fault, of course. Collymore's feeble effort from distance in the 11th minute trickled along the turf before hitting a rogue divot and bouncing over Flowers' head into the net.

Collymore, who cracked a smile but toned down his celebrations, turned away in disbelief as Flowers stared down at the pitch with his hands on his hips.

Liverpool went on to win the game 3-2 and Flowers described it as 'one of those ridiculous situations'.

Stan Collymore scored one of the strangest goals when his effort bobbled over Tim Flowers

Gary Neville (England vs Croatia) - October 11, 2006

Strange bobbles take me back to Gary Neville’s own goal in Zagreb. Early in the doomed England reign of Steve McClaren.

Neville rolled a simple back pass towards Paul Robinson who took a mighty swing at fresh air with his right boot and looked aghast as it trundled past him and into the net for Croatia's second in a 2-0 win. The Spurs keeper stamped furiously at the offending divot as the Maksimir Stadium erupted.

Adding another layer to the comic value were pitchside LED ad screens flashing up images of Sacha Baron Cohen’s new Borat film and one of his lame catchphrases: 'I like you'.

It was a bad omen at the start of the failed Euro 2008 campaign and the beginning of the end for both Robinson and Neville in England colours.

Gary Neville's own goal against Croatia came after Paul Robinson totally missed the ball

Stefan Kiessling (Hoffenheim v Leverkusen) - October 18, 2013

Legendary Bayer Leverkusen forward Stefan Kiessling has got to be one of the only players to score with a shot off target.

While away to Hoffenheim, a corner was swung in towards Leverkusen striker Kiessling, who, at first glance, simply headed home smartly.

But on closer inspection we can see that the ball was destined for the side netting and an inconspicuous hole in the side of the net let the ball slip in.

Even Kiessling himself had his head in his hands thinking he’d missed before turning around to see his teammates were celebrating.

Leverkusen's Stefan Kiessling must be one of the only players to score with a shot off target

#961. Jensen Huang: Spy row, affairs leave Nvidia without its rockstar CEO

Jensen Huang, who built Nvidia into the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, is stepping down as CEO over extramarital affairs. DW examines how losing its figurehead will affect the firm and the US-China AI race.

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The New York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

Those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

Megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators.  Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

Kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who currently works in the firm's robotics division.

Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the company and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," said Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the company for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the company so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

#960. Iranian activist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Narges Mohammadi shares her story in memoir

Written and smuggled out of prison, the 2023 Nobel Prize laureate's memoir reveals the cost of defying Iran's regime and fighting for freedom.

As PEN International marks Imprisoned Writer Day on November 15, a memoir by 2023 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Narges Mohammadi stands as a powerful act of resistance against authoritarian regimes.

"A Woman Never Stops Fighting — My Struggle for Freedom, Democracy and Human Rights in Iran," was recently published in German and is set to be released in English in September 2027.

The autobiography "portrays how Narges actually became the woman she is today — and it also reveals the price she had to pay to become that woman," Mariam Claren, spokesperson for the Narges Mohammadi Foundation Germany told DW.

Mohammadi wrote the autobiography in prison: "She was constantly writing," says Claren, whose own mother, activist Nahid Taghavi, shared a cell with Mohammadi for two and a half years, in Iran's notorious Evin prison. "Then, in 2020, Narges was forcibly moved to another prison. All her documents were gone. And she had to start all over."

But she managed to rewrite it all, and her texts were smuggled out of prison in fragments by fellow prisoners and visitors who risked their own safety.

In her memoir, Mohammadi recounts pivotal moments in her life, including her childhood and youth, how she started taking action against gender discrimination, political repression, the death penalty and human rights abuses, and the personal and emotional toll of her activism.

The human rights activist has been sentenced to a combined total of more than 44 years in prison and 154 lashes. For more than a decade, she has been separated from her twin children, who are now 19 years old and live in exile in France for their own protection.

Born on April 21, 1972, in Zanjan, Iran, Narges Mohammadi became politically active while studying in physics at Imam Khomeini University of Qazvin in the 1990s.

In "A Woman Never Stops Fighting," she describes how she started mountain climbing as a student, and organized mixed-gender groups dedicated to mountaineering — a controversial initiative at the time. She also helped establish an independent student organization and advocated for political reform. Her activities led to repeated harassment and arrests by authorities.

She began her journalism career in 1996, writing about Iran's student and women's movements. As her public profile grew, she became increasingly involved in Iran's civil society and human rights community.

In 1998, she married political activist Taghi Rahmani. The couple's twins, Ali and Kiana, were born in 2006.

Over the course of her career, Mohammadi worked with some of Iran's most prominent human rights organizations and became a leading figure in the Defenders of Human Rights Centre, founded by 2003 Nobel Peace Prize laureate Shirin Ebadi.

She played a key role in initiatives promoting free elections, peace and the abolition of the death penalty, especially for juvenile offenders. She also helped establish organizations supporting political prisoners and advocating for women's rights.

Her first major prison sentence related to her human rights activities came in 2011. It marked the beginning of a cycle of arrests and prosecutions that would define much of her adult life.

In her memoir, she describes an arrest that took place in front of her young children. At one point during her imprisonment, she lost the right to call them for several months.

She also details the brutal treatment she experienced in prison, with constant interrogations, beatings and denial of medical care.

Another central focus of her activism is denouncing the psychological effects of solitary confinement, which she had previously documented with fellow inmates in her book and documentary project "White Torture."

"When someone is subjected to physical torture, the scars, blood and infections — dreadful as they may be — serve as visible witnesses," she writes in her memoir. But, she adds, "when someone is subjected to psychological torture, no visible traces remain, and the victim cannot justify the trauma — neither to themselves nor to others. In fact, it becomes virtually impossible to even accept that one has been tortured at all, which causes the suffering to continue indefinitely."

"This is also the goal of solitary confinement: to bring the imprisoned person to the very edge of nothingness — to strip them of their identity and of everything that makes them human," she writes.

Through her relentless campaigning against executions and state violence, she helped bring these issues to the forefront of public debate among Iranian activists.

International recognition of her work culminated in October 2023 when she was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for "for her fight against the oppression of women in Iran and her fight to promote human rights and freedom for all."

As Mohammadi was unable to attend the ceremony because she remained imprisoned in Tehran's Evin Prison, the award was accepted on her behalf by her teenage twins, who delivered her message to the world.

Following the Nobel Prize, Iranian authorities continued to pursue new legal cases against her, restrict her communications and intensify pressure on her from prison.

She became the target of a systematic smear campaign, including widespread defamation, gender-based harassment and explicit death threats.

"We are firmly convinced that the Islamic Republic of Iran has deployed its cyber army — which is the second-largest, after Russia's — to this end," says Claren of the Narges Mohammadi Foundation. Conspiracy theorists even started claiming she might be working for the regime, she adds: "And what is truly terrible about this is that when a lie is repeated over and over again and spread over the course of years, it eventually leads even ordinary people to start believing it."

In late 2024, following surgery, Mohammadi was granted a temporary medical release. Doctors warned at the time that a return to prison could seriously endanger her health.

Nevertheless, Mohammadi was brutally arrested again in December 2025, while attending a memorial ceremony for Khosrow Alikordi, a lawyer and human rights activist who died in suspicious circumstances.

In prison, she was held in solitary confinement for an extended period and her health continued to deteriorate, Claren reports. But "thanks to a public campaign, she has now been granted what is known as an interruption of detention for medical reasons."

But "that doesn't mean she is free," adds Claren, who notes that she still suffers from serious health problems — as do many Iranians who have been tortured in prison.

In February, an Iranian court ordered additional prison sentences for Mohammadi, along with a travel ban.

Mohammadi lives in constant fear of having to return to prison any day, notes Claren, and "this all comes with the pressure to which Iranian civil society — including, of course, people like Narges — is currently subjected, with questions like: Will Trump launch an attack, yes or no? Will there be another war?"

Despite this uncertainty, Mohammadi continues her activism. Her international profile also helps her supporters keep addressing publicly the issue of human rights in Iran in the public eye, says Claren: "It is incredibly important that, alongside the individual Narges Mohammadi, the focus also remains consistently on the struggle of the people in Iran for freedom, dignity, and fundamental rights — for the right to sing and dance."

#959. A guide to the Nature Index

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The Nature Index is a database of author affiliations and institutional relationships. The index tracks contributions to research articles published in high-quality natural-science and health-science journals, chosen based on reputation by an independent group of researchers.

The Nature Index provides absolute and fractional counts of article publication at the institutional and national level and, as such, is an indicator of global high-quality research output and collaboration. Data in the Nature Index are updated regularly, with the most recent 12 months made available under a Creative Commons licence at natureindex.com. The database is compiled by Nature Portfolio.

The Nature Index uses Count and Share to track research output. A country/territory or an institution is given a Count of 1 for each article that has at least one author from that country/territory or institution. This is the case regardless of the number of authors an article has, and it means that the same article can contribute to the Count of multiple countries/territories or institutions.

To glean a country’s, territory’s, region’s or an institution’s contribution to an article, and to ensure that they are not counted more than once, the Nature Index uses Share, a fractional count that takes into account the share of authorship on each article. The total Share available per article is 1, which is shared among all authors under the assumption that each contributed equally. For instance, an article with 10 authors means that each author receives a Share of 0.1. For authors who are affiliated with more than one institution, the author’s Share is split equally between each institution. The total Share for an institution is calculated by summing the Share for individual affiliated authors. The process is similar for countries/territories, although complicated by the fact that some institutions have overseas labs that will be counted towards host country/territory totals.

Adjusted Share accounts for the annual variation in the total number of articles in the Nature Index journals. It is arrived at by calculating the percentage difference in the total number of articles in the Index in a given year relative to the number of articles in a base year and adjusting Share values to the base year levels.

The bilateral collaboration score (CS) between two institutions A+B is the sum of each of their Shares on the papers to which both have contributed. A bilateral collaboration can be between any two institutions or countries/territories co-authoring at least one article in the journals tracked by the Nature Index.

natureindex.com users can search for specific institutions or countries and generate their own reports, ordered by Count or Share.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03474-5

Bullied by Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey, then by Leeds United’s Dominic Calvert-Lewin. Liam Delap, of all people, is probably the last striker that Chelsea’s defenders want to be facing next.

A striker who is seen as something of a brutish throwback. A striker with a point to prove versus his old employers who were happy to sell him after a single season. A striker who will know, having trained with Levi Colwill and Wesley Fofana, how to make this an uncomfortable match.

Delap will lead the line for Nottingham Forest, and as if Colwill and Co needed any additional spotlight on them, this Premier League encounter will take place on Friday under the lights of the City Ground – about as intimidating a setting as they could have asked for.

Chelsea have conceded 20 Premier League goals this season. It is as many as they have scored, and so as much as we applauded their attacking earlier this term, we must likewise scrutinise the defending to the same degree.

Daily Mail Sport watched back all 20 to analyse, see who was at fault and issue each a Keystone Cops rating. Yes, there have been some 10 out of 10s.

Chelsea have conceded 20 goals already in the Premier League after losing 4-1 at home to Leeds. Pictured: Noah Okafor scores Leeds first goal in their win at Stamford Bridge

Xabi Alonso's defence must be scrutinised over the nature of the goals they are conceding

1 – Fulham, Josh King, 23rd minute, for 1-1

Xabi Alonso’s first taste of a setback on day one. All King had to do was make a run behind Morgan Rogers, whose defensive awareness was on show with England in the last international break but less so here for Chelsea. King blasted on an angle and from 16 yards, and Robert Sanchez was beaten at his near post as Alonso clocked why this goalkeeper is not for him.

2 – Fulham, Gonzalo Garcia, 54th minute, for 3-2 to Chelsea

While Chelsea binned Sanchez and replaced him with Emiliano Martinez after this game, this goal involved an error from a centre-back, first and foremost. Colwill failed to deal with a long ball, heading fresh air rather than clearing, then Sanchez spilled his save for Garcia’s rebound.

3 – Brighton, Malick Yalcouye, 35th minute, for 3-1 to Chelsea

This originated from a long throw taken quickly in Brighton’s own half and sent down the line. Pedro Neto flew across to try to tackle on the wing, but forgot to take the actual ball. Yalcouye charged forward and played in Charalampos Kostoulas, who ran behind Maxence Lacroix. His shot was saved, but Yalcouye finished with oomph as the ball pinged in off the post.

4 – Brighton, Joao Pedro own goal, 63rd minute, for 3-2 to Chelsea

An unfortunate deflection from Joao Pedro as Pascal Gross took aim. In the build-up, Cole Palmer neglected his defensive duties by allowing Gross to run behind him, much like Rogers v Fulham the week before. The nick from Joao Pedro wrongfooted Martinez in goal. It happens.

Chelsea's vulnerabilities were on show as they overcame Brighton 4-3 back in August

5 – Brighton, Pascal Gross, 96th minute, for 4-3 to Chelsea

A long throw. A spot of head tennis with Valentin Barco initially beaten in the air by Diego Gomez. Then Gross nods beyond Martinez as Joao Pedro asks Rogers why he didn’t have him. A soft consolation to concede.

6 – Arsenal, Kai Havertz, 25th minute, for 1-1

This one was largely on the goalkeeping as a few wondered whether Martinez was Sanchez in disguise. Havertz dashed inside from the right wing and away from Fofana, then scored from 18 yards into the small sliver of light available at Martinez’s near post. With that, Chelsea's lead was lost.

7 – Arsenal, Martin Odegaard, 50th minute, for 2-1 to Arsenal

Sometimes, you just have to say the opposition's move worked well, and this was a fine one from Arsenal rather than a defensive disasterclass per se, even if Fofana was fooled by Havertz’s dummy. That allowed the pass from Christos Tzolis to roll through to Odegaard to score the winner after Reece James had not spied how his fellow captain was unmarked in front of him.

8 – Hull, Mohamed Belloumi, 28th minute, for 1-1

Do not let the ball bounce. That is defending 101. The no-no we are all taught as kids. Jorrel Hato broke that basic rule here. Hato let the ball bounce in front of him and loop over him after it was launched into the box from the left wing by Ryan Giles, with Chelsea’s other full back Malo Gusto having failed to stop that cross from coming. Belloumi was waiting behind Hato to score. Hato was hooked at half-time for good reason.

Mohamed Belloumi scored the first of two goals for Hull against the Blues after Jorrel Hato allowed the ball to bounce in the box

9 – Hull, Mohamed Belloumi, 34th minute, for 2-1 to Hull

Martinez came to clear Hull's corner. He didn’t. He flapped as Semi Ajayi, who did not even have a marker on him as Colwill and Fofana were marking zonally rather than taking care of the 6ft 4in centre-back, headed into the crossbar. The rebound fell to Belloumi, who, unmarked at the edge of the box, scored via two deflections which made Chelsea’s six-yard box resemble a pinball machine. Not a good look for Austin MacPhee, the new set-piece specialist.

10 – Brentford, Jaidon Anthony, 61st minute, for 1-0 to Brentford

Another one which MacPhee will want to leave off the showreel. The corner came in. It went to the back of the pack. It was headed back across by Jannik Schuster, then in by Anthony. Fofana, Lacroix and Danny Welbeck formed a nice little triangle around the attacker without anyone ever actually marking him.

11 – Brentford, Igor Thiago, 83rd minute, for 2-0 to Brentford

Jordan Henderson tried and failed to punch a pass forward. It turned over possession, and Brentford countered. Chelsea had a high line as they were pushing for the equaliser, which was understandable. One lovely through-ball from Mikkel Damsgaard later, Kevin Schade was through. Martinez denied him one-v-one, but Thiago finished the rebound.

12 – Brentford, Fabio Carvalho, 94th minute, for 3-0 to Brentford

It originated from a long throw, cleared partially by Chelsea but recycled to the wing by Brentford. A low cross came in with a deflection from Josh Acheampong helping it find Carvalho, who had sneaked in behind Pep Chavarria.

Fabio Carvalho scored Brentford's final goal in their 3-0 win in September after sneaking in at the back post, after Chelsea only partially cleared from a long throw

13 – Bournemouth, Evanilson, 51st minute, for 3-1 to Chelsea

Never let it be said that Chelsea do not give confidence to strikers. Evanilson had not scored in the Premier League since February 2026. Then he visited Stamford Bridge in this fixture in October. Since then, he has scored in every league game played, now on six in a row. This goal came from a Bournemouth corner. It was flicked on at the front of the pack. Moises Caicedo tried to clear the ball amid a goalmouth melee, but only blasted his clearance into Evanilson for a gimme of a goal.

14 – Tottenham, Mike Penders own goal, 77th minute, for 1-0 to Tottenham

Whatever you do, when starting in the Premier League for the first time and against your side’s fiercest rivals no less, do not punch the ball into your own goal. Anyway, Penders came for a corner, and you know what happened next. It did not help that the 21-year-old goalkeeper was challenged by Jan Paul van Hecke, who was allowed a free run at him after being left by Lacroix, but even so. This was a horrific moment for Penders, and happened despite Chelsea trying that trick where they send players out of the box to ease the congestion.

15 – Tottenham, Mathys Tel, 87th minute, for 2-0 to Tottenham

Acheampong lost the ball over on the right wing and couldn’t catch up with Tel as he flew forward. There was a weak attempt at a tackle by Lacroix, who almost sheepishly stuck out a lazy leg. Then Tel scored from 25 yards as Alonso violated a non-negotiable: you do not lose at home to Tottenham.

Mike Penders punched a corner into his own net as Chelsea suffered a rare home loss to Tottenham

16 – Sunderland, Enzo Le Fee, 36th minute, for 1-0 to Sunderland

A penalty, but we will analyse the build-up. Colwill in particular had been getting bullied by Brobbey in this game. So much so that he went on to be hooked at half-time while on a yellow. On this occasion, Sunderland launched a long ball towards Brobbey, who used his strength to turn Colwill and charge into the box. He then dropped down – controversially so as Chelsea did not believe it warranted a spot-kick. Le Fee stepped up, and scored the game’s only goal.

17 – Leeds, Noah Okafor, 28th minute, for 1-1

Chelsea fans could take their pick of players to blame here. First, there was Fofana not heading back James Trafford’s long ball from whence it came. One of Willie Isa’s jobs as Chelsea’s ‘cultural architect’ is to act as a human shield while the defenders practise winning headers in their warm-up. They still seem to mess up a fair few mid-match, as Fofana did here. Then there was Acheampong letting the ball bounce over him à la Hato, and Colwill backtracking as if stuck in reverse. All three were surrounding Okafor as he then made it 1-1. Martinez did not even attempt to dive as the ball rolled by him. Colwill appeared to ask him why as Leeds celebrated. Excruciating by everyone involved.

18 – Leeds, Dominic Calvert-Lewin, 53rd minute, for 2-1 to Leeds

Another penalty, but one which we believe should not have been awarded for a handball by Rogers. It was given by Michael Oliver in real time, and backed up by Michael Salisbury on VAR. Any reasonable fan would hate it if this was given against their club. Anyway, it all originated from a long throw. Three Chelsea players tried to head it clear at the same time – good communication, lads – and they failed as Fofana only flicked it on behind him. What followed was this gift of a spot-kick, which Calvert-Lewin scored for 2-1.

19 – Leeds, Noah Okafor, 58th minute, for 3-1 to Leeds

Yet more ball-watching from Chelsea’s defenders as opposed to taking note of the chap that had already scored one goal lining up for his second. Okafor was always unmarked as he moved into the box from around the penalty spot to meet Ethan Ampadu’s deflected cross.

20 – Leeds, Brenden Aaronson, 91st minute, for 4-1 to Leeds

A ball forward from Leeds left Colwill in a bind. Because he was supposed to have both Calvert-Lewin and Harry Wilson, he was stuck in between, and actually had neither. Calvert-Lewin headed to Wilson, who had time to pick his pass. Gusto, on as a substitute, noticed Aaronson making a burst in behind Chelsea’s back line. He tried to play him offside by suddenly stopping running with him but timed it wrong. Aaronson was onside. Gusto raced to try to stop him, but the Leeds attacker simply checked back inside, and scored through the legs of Martinez, who gave the woodwork a kicking in frustration.

#957. England stun world champions Spain in one of their greatest victories

Thomas Tuchel may not have planned it this way, but in one night he gave us all the rich history of the England team at once: some glorious attacking football, some self-sabotage defending, a red card, a late siege and a fight.

This was the beguiling story of Spain 2 England 3, an evening that began with the world champions parading the World Cup trophy and ended with 10 Englishmen defending a lead with their last breath. England beat the world champions in Madrid, and for more than 30 minutes including injury time they did so with 10 men, Dan Burn heading the last ball out as per the tradition of a defensive rearguard action.

This was the game that had it all: including a substitute, in Djed Spence, who had already picked up a yellow card on the bench before he came on. It was a coming-of-age performance in goal for James Trafford. So too for Ben White, the 2022 World Cup departee who scored the third and lunged with astonishing effect in the 84th minute to block a Nico Williams shot.

Trafford again! 👊🏻 An excellent double save from the Leeds United keeper 🙌 https://t.co/L27oQFQO1J

This was a performance good enough to win a World Cup final, never mind Nations League Group A3 – just a shame England neglected to get to that World Cup final in the summer. The fight in question was at half-time as the players came off and White and Fabián Ruiz first tangled and others dived in.

There was so much to admire. England began the night testing Spain’s first-phase passing to breaking point. They began the second half counter-attacking Spain for two goals from Ezri Konsa and White. Then after Elliot Anderson’s red card, this was a different England. With Trafford in inspired form, they held off the relentless Spain for long enough.

Harry Kane scored his 93rd England goal from the spot and was replaced before the end so that Myles Lewis-Skelly’s energy could give the midfield one more lease of life. By the end, the excitement meant that Kane was unable to take his seat on the bench, and he stood alongside Tuchel in the technical area, cajoling and advising.

England have beaten Spain on Spanish territory in recent times, but it was the nature of this performance, its many qualities when the moment required them, that made it so significant. This was the end of a 43-game unbeaten streak for the European and world champions, and it was ended by an England team in their best form in recent years.

Only three who started this game – Kane, Jude Bellingham and Declan Rice – started the final of Euro 2024, lost to Spain. Tuchel’s pool of talent is deeper than it was for his predecessor but there is also a greater maturity to the way they play. The England manager called it the greatest performance of almost two years in charge “given the circumstances… who we play, where we play” and as ever for England just slightly too late.

The defeat by Argentina in the semi-final in Atlanta just stings that little bit more when one considers the craft and resilience England showed on this night. They were under the hammer after Anderson threw an arm over the shoulder of Lamine Yamal and was dismissed before Mikel Oyarzabal converted the penalty that followed. “Thirty minutes against Spain in Spain feels like three hours,” Tuchel said, although Spain had a long way back after the blitzing they took at times in the first hour.

They all had their moments. Anthony Gordon had a strong first half. Morgan Rogers was central to the two goals England scored in the 10 minutes after the break. Anderson demonstrated that he is one of the best midfielders in the world in the hour before his red card. Spain were without Rodri and in his absence his Manchester City successor was in control.

Tuchel encouraged his players to mount a ferocious press against the best first-phase passing team in the world. Brave, but it worked beautifully and for an absorbing opening 10 minutes, Spain looked all at sea. Such was the pressure, the Spain goalkeeper Unai Simón abandoned the usual build-up strategy and launched his goal-kicks to the halfway line.

Even when Spain finally found their rhythm at the mid-point of the first half, England adapted. It took them a while to manage the discomfort of being denied the ball, and the familiar rapid incursions and switches of play. The counter-attacking switch from the early period pressing Spain in their own area yielded the penalty from which Kane scored the first.

Thomas Tuchel praised England’s “statement win” that ended Spain’s 43-game unbeaten run and secured top spot ahead of the world champions in the Nations League.

Tuchel and Declan Rice revealed they had both believed England would end Spain’s long unbeaten streak, and their confidence proved well-founded.

“This was of course a statement victory,” Tuchel said. “I’m happy the players felt so confident. I felt it as well. I also had the same belief [that England would win]. I think we felt it from each other.

“The result followed the performance. I think it was on the highest level in terms of belief, team spirit, togetherness and it was on the highest level football-wise, in all aspects of the game.”

Tuchel described the nature of England’s win as “the Azteca reloaded” in reference to the World Cup victory over Mexico, but felt the win in Madrid was the best of his reign as head coach.

He said: “Yeah [it was the best performance of his reign so far], given the circumstances and the pressure and the quality and where we played and playing against the reigning world champions. They were unbeaten in 43 games. So putting a performance out there in Madrid, in this environment, that was a very complete performance and the best I’ve had so far.

“The last half an hour felt like Azteca reloaded, to be honest. Again, it was a beautiful week. The commitment to get better is on the highest level.

“I said it many times, I love these players and I love the mentality .We’re building something and that was the next step. It was an amazing atmosphere. I will bottle it up for sure and then unfortunately we have to wait until the quarter-final.”

“We had a fantastic result and performance in Croatia followed up by a very good performance at home against Czechia. We then got our homework done against Croatia three days ago and that’s what we always wanted.

“We wanted to come back and compete on the highest level and see how far we can push our limits and how far we can push the opponent with the way we want to play and stay true to our identity. The team did excellent.”

Thomas Tuchel will speak openly to England’s players about what they should do if they encounter racism in the Nations League Group 3 decider with Spain.

This is the first time England have faced Spain in Madrid since November 2004 when they were beaten 1-0 in the Santiago Bernabéu, a game that was ravaged by obscene chanting. The nations were supposed to play a fixture in the Spanish capital in 2008, but the Football Association insisted it be moved to Seville instead.

Earlier this year, Spanish supporters brought shame on themselves again after a flurry of anti-Muslim chants marred a friendly against Egypt; they were fined $20,000 by Fifa and must play their next friendly in a partially closed stadium.

There will be a full house in the Wanda Metropolitano on Sunday night, as the reigning world and European champions aim to defend their extraordinary unbeaten run of 43 games, and England head coach Tuchel is adamant the atmosphere will be in keeping with the occasion.

The German has, however, made it clear he and his staff will use their platform before the contest to remind England’s players of the steps they should take if the worst scenario unfolds.

Asked about incidents that had pockmarked this fixture before, Tuchel said: “I think I hear it the first time that this happens. I think it’s unacceptable. In any stadium, not even in stadiums, we will never accept racism. We will never be racist towards anyone.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of England’s final Nations League Group 3 decider as Thomas Tuchel’s side take on Spain at Metropolitano Stadium in Madrid.

Although both countries are safely through to the quarter-finals, England will seek revenge on Spain, who beat them in the Euro 2024 final and in their previous Nations League face-off on September 26 at Wembley. That day, Luis de la Fuente’s men profited from Harry Kane’s uncharacteristic penalty miss, England’s general wastefulness in front of goal and some seriously lacklustre defending to earn a chaotic 3-2 comeback victory after falling 2-1 behind at half-time.

Since that defeat, England have won four successive Nations League fixtures against the Czech Republic and Croatia by an aggregate score of 14-1. Last time out, they beat Croatia on Thursday, earning a 2-1 win as Kane, who became England’s most-capped men’s player with 126 appearances, dispatched a second-half penalty to seal the three points. Spearheaded by the Ballon d’Or holder’s brilliance, England must win this evening in order to overtake Spain and top the group.

#956. Could lack of money sink TFFF rainforest fund before it even launches?

The TFFF rainforest fund aims to make forest conservation more profitable than deforestation. But a lack of money may prevent it from getting off the ground.

The world's tropical forests play a vital role in slowing global heating and preserving biodiversity, storing climate-damaging carbon dioxide and providing a home for an extremely large number of species — when they're intact.

More than 140 countries committed to halting global deforestation by the end of the decade at the 2021 UN climate change conference in Glasgow, but five years later logging continues.

In 2024, over 8 million hectares (19 million acres) of forest were lost. And since 1990, nearly 490 million hectares of forest have been wiped out.

More recently, the trend has shifted in the opposite direction. Deforestation in the Amazon region of Brazil decreased by 41% from August 2025 through 2026 to reach its lowest rate since records began.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

To ensure lasting protection, the Tropical Forest Forever Facility was launched in 2025 at the COP30 climate conference in Belem, Brazil.

Because rainforests are so important for the world, the idea behind the fund was to give money to the countries where they are located to help them preserve and protect these ecosystems.

So far, these countries have made more profit through deforestation — for example, by mining natural resources on rainforest land or farming the area.

Starting in 2027, the TFFF is expected to generate the funds needed for rainforest conservation, in part via contributions from various countries. By the end of this year, a total of $10 billion (€8.9 billion) in government capital is due to flow into the fund, mainly in the form of low-interest loans.

In addition, the TFFF is expected to issue bonds to private investors, such as banks and investment firms, to raise additional funds — initially totaling about $40 billion.

Going forward, the plan is for governments to contribute a total of $25 billion to the pot, and for private donors to contribute $100 billion. The fund will then invest this money in international financial markets with the aim of generating profits.

Private investors who purchase TFFF bonds can expect to earn about 5% interest per bond per year, said Felix Finkbeiner, the founder of the German environmental organization Plant-for-the-Planet, where he is responsible for forest conservation and advocacy.

"Private investors' capital is very well protected," Finkbeiner said, adding that any losses the TFFF might incur on the capital markets — for example, if the price of its bonds should fall — would be offset by government funds.

About 2.7% of the TFFF's profits would be set aside for countries with tropical forests.

Countries would receive $4 per year for every hectare of forest that they preserve instead of chopping down. At least 20% of these funds must be allocated to Indigenous peoples and local communities.

According to calculations by the TFFF Watch website, an independent platform launched by Plant-for-the-Planet to track investments, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for example, would receive about $333 million for its 2024 forest stock under this system.

Finkbeiner said the subsidies would be paid only for intact ecosystems and not for timber plantations, with forest areas and their condition mapped and assessed using satellite imagery. Though it can sometimes be difficult to identify plantations accurately on satellite photos, he said, the technology has improved significantly over the last decade.

That means any NGO or external party with access to the satellite data can check the condition of the region, providing further oversight. If forest areas are cleared or damaged, money is deducted from the total.

Another safeguard: If countries don't use the TFFF funds for rainforest conservation, their payments could be frozen for the next few years.

The TFFF is supposed to invest, whenever possible, in government bonds issued by emerging and developing countries. Above all, the idea is not to invest in projects that harm the climate — such as those linked to oil, gas, or coal investments.

The TFFF concept has received plenty of support from environmental organizations, in part because it gives countries in the Global South significantly more sovereignty than traditional forms of development financing.

"For example, if the government of Ghana wants to protect its rainforest today, it usually asks the World Bank for financial assistance — and then the World Bank in [Washington] DC decides whether Ghana is allowed to do so," Finkbeiner said.

The TFFF fund is also designed to be immune to donor countries' backing out in the event of a change in government, for example. Once a contribution is made, the money remains in the fund for 40 years before being paid back.

Continuing protection is also an incentive for countries receiving money from the fund. "When a new government comes into power that wants to cut back a little on climate protection, they will realize: We'll get more money if we protect the rainforest," said Finkbeiner.

For the rainforest fund to actually get off the ground, a total of $10 billion in seed capital must be raised by the end of 2026. So far, the confirmed pledges from countries, NGOs and foundations total only $7.9 billion.

Eight countries have expressed a willingness to contribute so far, including Brazil, Indonesia, France, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands and Luxembourg.

Norway, with a pledge of $3 billion, is the largest would-be donor. However, the government in Oslo is willing to honor its commitment only if the agreed-upon total amount is in place by the end of the year.

"This deadline isn't set in stone, but otherwise the Norwegian government will have real trouble getting it through parliament," Finkbeiner said.

Germany's commitment must also still be approved by the parliament. The German government has pledged about €1 billion to the TFFF starting in 2027, to be paid out over 10 years.

Other countries are also considering investing in the TFFF, including Canada, China, South Korea and the United Arab Emirates.

Philanthropic organizations have pledged $88 million to the fund so far, including $73 million announced this week during the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Finkbeiner remains upbeat.

"Promises like that always come at the last minute," he said. "I'm very optimistic that we'll secure more commitments at the COP — and in the course of December — and that we'll then reach that $10 billion."

This article was originally written in German.

#950. The world has a golden chance to improve HIV prevention: don’t squander it

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

South Africa’s health officials at the launch in June of lenacapavir, a drug that provides strong protection against HIV when administered twice a year.Credit: Per-Anders Pettersson/Getty

Earlier this month, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved a generic version of the HIV drug lenacapavir for use as a preventive treatment. Twice-yearly injections of this game-changing medicine — originally developed by the company Gilead Sciences in Foster City, California — have been shown to be more than 95% effective at preventing HIV acquisition1. At the same time, as Nature reports in a News feature, an HIV vaccine — that would ultimately be a more robust solution to preventing HIV — is closer than ever before.

A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies

A powerful HIV vaccine is finally within reach — thanks to these super antibodies

In 2024, Gilead signed licensing agreements with six pharmaceutical companies, allowing them to make and sell generic versions of lenacapavir in 120 low- and middle-income countries, subject to regulatory approval. The recent FDA approval brings access a step closer in these countries. The cost to users has been set at US$40 per year, fuelling hopes that the drug will help to bring the global HIV epidemic under control.

These welcome developments contrast with the situation of public funding for HIV research and treatment, which is reeling from deep and unconscionable cuts from the US government. Many of the researchers whom Nature spoke to for the News feature had been funded by a programme for preclinical HIV-vaccine research run by the US National Institutes of Health (NIH). But the agency ended the programme last year, forcing researchers to scale back their research and seek alternative funding. Whatever funding comes next is likely to be less stable and less predictable than the NIH funding. It’s imperative that the cuts be reversed — or new government funding sources found.

The path to an HIV vaccine has been long and bumpy, with decades of high-profile and costly failures, but there is now light at the end of the tunnel. The latest strategy — known as germline targeting — is designed to trigger the production of rare, highly potent antibodies that can prevent infection with diverse HIV strains. The technique has shown encouraging results in animal models2–4 and in early trials in humans5. Researchers are more optimistic than they’ve been in years that an effective HIV vaccine could be on the horizon.

The end of AIDS is in sight: don’t abandon PEPFAR now

The end of AIDS is in sight: don’t abandon PEPFAR now

But in the meantime, antiretroviral drugs such as lenacapavir look poised to have a big impact on infection prevention. In Africa alone, new infections could be cut by around one-third if just 5% of adults most likely to acquire HIV received the drug, and by half if it was given to one-fifth of adults, according to the Gates Foundation’s Institute for Disease Modelling in Seattle, Washington.

But lenacapavir alone is unlikely to bring the HIV epidemic fully under control. There are several reasons for this: first, it’s not always easy to determine who needs the drug most. Second, to be effective, the drug must be taken for most of someone’s life — or at least while they are sexually active. Third, even $40 a year is unaffordable for people on the very lowest incomes.

Until recently, the United States was the stand-out funder for antiretroviral drugs for people living with HIV in low-and middle-income countries. That stopped in January 2025, when the US administration suspended funding. Although it later restored a limited amount, the effects have been devastating. A survey published earlier this year found that some 1,700 facilities previously offering treatments to people living with HIV had closed as a result (see go.nature.com/4a7ftp4).

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Trump blew up the global fight against AIDS. Can it recover?

Such instability highlights the importance of vaccines. “The funding cuts that happened in the past couple of years have really made it even more obvious how fragile that system of reliance” on drug access is, says Penny Moore, a virologist at South Africa’s National Institute for Communicable Disease in Johannesburg. And that fragility, as Rogier Sanders, an HIV-vaccine researcher at Amsterdam University Medical Centre, says, is why research into a vaccine remains a priority: “A vaccine makes you independent from access to drugs.”

But the US cuts have not only curtailed the preclinical vaccine programme, they have also forced the postponement and scaling back of an HIV vaccine trial in South Africa. They have also affected supporting research, such as surveillance efforts tracking HIV evolution in African countries, says Nairobi-based Vincent Muturi-Kioi, who is leading development of HIV vaccines at the International AIDS Vaccine Initiative in New York City.

Success stories such as the repurposing of lenacapavir as a preventive treatment and progress in vaccine development show the importance of investment in health. It is imperative that HIV vaccine research and deployment continues to receive support, at the same time as rolling out lenacapavir as widely as possible.

It could take more than a decade to translate the encouraging results with germline targeting into an effective HIV vaccine, and the current strategy might encounter more hurdles.

The world is closer than it has ever been to an effective HIV vaccine and has a drug capable of preventing infections. Now is the time for funders to ramp up investment, not cut it back.

#949. Hearts 2-3 Monaco: Late agony for brave hosts in Conference League tie - as Folarin Balogun strikes at the death to settle rollercoaster Tynecastle epic

Published: 15:54 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 17:41 EST, 26 November 2026

On a pulsating but ultimately painful evening for Hearts, their bid to reach the knockout phase of the UEFA Conference League suffered an agonising 94th-minute blow after they had gone toe-to-toe with a classy Monaco side.

USA World Cup striker Folarin Balogun’s stoppage-time winner preserved the Ligue 1 club’s perfect record in the league stage of the tournament and leaves Wouter Vrancken’s men with no remaining room for error.

Hearts must now win their last two games next month, at home to Bosnian side Borac and away to Pafos in Cyprus, to finish on seven points which could still be enough to secure a top 24 place in the 36-team standings.

It was a sickening conclusion to a thrilling match which saw Jordi Altena and Sabah Kerjota both score goal-of-the-season contenders for Hearts in a rollercoaster first half in which Balogun and Edan Diop were on target for Monaco.

Hearts emerged from the night with plenty of credit for their bold and often enterprising approach but it is points rather than plaudits they now need if their European campaign is to carry on beyond Christmas.

This would have been a challenging assignment for Hearts under any circumstances but the degree of difficulty was increased for Vrancken’s side by their injury list.

USA striker Folarin Balogun celebrates the late goal that broke hearts at Tynecastle

While easing slightly in recent weeks, with Blair Spittal the latest welcome returnee as he took a place on the bench, it remains significant and the Hearts coach was only able to name six outfield players among his subs.

With winger Josh McPake a surprising omission from the starting line-up, Vrancken sought greater solidity with the inclusion of 19-year-old defensive midfielder Matty Gillies.

After two sub outings since being recalled from his loan at Stenhousemuir, it was a baptism of fire for the teenager as he made his first start for Hearts.

Along with his more experienced team-mates, Gillies was chasing shadows for the opening ten minutes or so as Monaco moved the ball around with pace, precision and real intent.

Matthis Abline was a real thorn in the side of the Hearts defence and there was an early warning sign when the striker cut them open and teed up a good chance for Takumi Minamino. The former Liverpool winger couldn’t get his shot away, instead scuffing the ball into the path of Diop whose effort was blocked.

It was looking ominous for Hearts at this stage, with Abline quickly surging clear again to set up Christian Mawissa for a shot which flew well over the top, but they gradually secured a foothold in the contest.

Monaco forward Balogun sends the ball beyond Beau Reus to settle a rollercoaster match

Pierre Landry Kabore was first to threaten for the hosts when he muscled his way into the Monaco penalty area but the big striker’s lack of finesse and awareness saw him drag a shot wide when he should have picked out Gillies in a more promising position.

Hearts grew in belief and made the 16th-minute breakthrough with their first wonder strike of the evening. Kerjota’s free-kick from around 20 yards was a decent enough hit, the ball rebounding off Lukas Hradecky’s left hand post.

Claudio Braga did well to keep possession for Hearts and found Altena on the edge of the box. The Dutch full-back displayed outstanding technique to smash a rising shot beyond the helpless Hradecky and send the home fans into raptures.

Monaco briefly appeared rattled and Hearts might have done more to take advantage of a mix-up between Hradecky and Sadibou Sane which saw Laurent Mendy nick the ball and find Kabore who again lacked the composure needed to get a shot on target.

Just as it seemed Hearts were in the ascendancy, however, they gifted Monaco an equaliser. It was another unhappy moment in Europe for Jamie McCart, who scored an own goal in Hearts’ previous game away to Swiss side Thun.

The defender caught Abline with a rash and clumsy challenge inside the box, leaving German referee Daniel Schlager with a simple decision to make as he pointed to the spot.

Jordi Altena turns to celebrate his exquisite opener that sent the Tynecastle crowd wild

Balogun stepped forward and calmly slotted the penalty low to the left of Beau Reus and into the corner of the net.

The goal sparked another spell of dominance from the visitors who were finding it all too easy to pass their way through central midfield where Gillies and Laurent Mendy were regularly outnumbered.

Balogun came close to finding the net again when he got in behind McCart on the left side of the penalty area before dragging a shot just wide from a difficult angle.

The visitors did take the lead in the 41st minute and, once more, Hearts were the architects of their own downfall. This time, they conceded possession cheaply from their own throw-in when Altena took one touch too many and gave the ball away.

Monaco ruthlessly made the most of the opening it presented as Balogun raced clear and set up the unmarked Diop for a simple close-range finish.

No sooner had they seized the initiative, however, Monaco found themselves back on level terms once again as Kerjota conjured up a stunning goal which was arguably even better than Altena’s opener.

Sabah Kerjota unleashes a ridiculous left-footed shot that sailed gracefully into the top corner

Sabri Guendouz, whose pace and direct running was a real headache for Monaco, did well to earn a free-kick on the left. Altena flighted it to the far post where Stuart Findlay won the aerial battle. The ball fell to Kerjota on the right corner of the penalty area and he curled a sumptuous shot beyond Hradecky into the top left corner of the net.

A remarkable first half almost ended with a third Hearts goal in stoppage time. Minamino, already booked, was fortunate to avoid a second yellow card when he tripped Guendouz on the edge of the box. Altena’s set piece expertise was called upon again and he was unlucky to see his dipping effort narrowly clear the crossbar.

Hearts had to defend smartly and bravely for long spells in the second half, no one doing it better than McCart who recovered brilliantly from his earlier setback as he produced several crucial interventions.

Reus had to make fine saves to deny Jordan Teze and Abline but Hearts had menacing moments of their own. Hopes were raised when the ref pointed to the spot for handball against Monaco sub Mathys Detourbet in the 71st minute but the award was rightly reversed by VAR.

Albanian winger Kerjota takes the acclaim of his team-mates before the late heartbreak

Rogers Mato made an astonishing goal-line clearance to prevent Detourbet scoring at the other end and it looked as if Hearts would hold on for a valuable point.

Then came the late, late heartbreak as Mamadou Coulibaly sent Balogun racing free to coolly slot the ball beyond Reus and leave Hearts’ prospects of further progress in the tournament hanging by a thread.

Hearts (4-2-3-1): Reus 7; Altena 7, McCart 7, Findlay 7, Borchgrevink 6 (Mato 46); Gillies 5 (Spittal 46), Mendy 6; Kerjota 8 (Pollock 81), Braga 6 (Wilson 85), Guendouz 7 (McPake 76); Kabore 6. Booked: Altena, Kabore. Manager: Wouter Vrancken 7.

Monaco (3-4-2-1): Hradecky 7; Sane 7, Dier 7, Teze 7; Vanderson 6 (Nazinho 57), Zakaria 6, Diop 6 (Coulibaly 64), Mawissa 6 (Detourbet 64); Minamino 6 (Belmokhtar 57), Abline 8 (Soubeir 87); Balogun 8. Booked: Abline, Minamino, Mawissa, Detourbet. Manager: Filipe Luis 7.

#947. Germany's Nmecha won't repeat controversial goal celebration

Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp has said midfielder Felix Nmecha will not repeat a goal celebration that sparked controversy over the past week. Germany are set to face Serbia and the Netherlands in the Nations League.

With the controversy sparked by Felix Nmecha's celebrations after his goals in Dortmund's 2-1 win over Elfersberg last weekend, the subject was always going to be top of reporters' minds when Germany coach Jürgen Klopp faced reporters ahead of Friday's match against Serbia.

Nmecha celebrated the goals by mimicking taking a crown off his head and kneeling to place it on the ground.

This was understood by many to be a nod to a Ballers in God (BIG) campaign called "The King's Return."

BIG, a Christian group for footballers, has said it aims to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone," but critics claim it discriminates against the queer and transexual people. The discourse generated by the celebration did not go unnoticed by the Germany boss.

​Klopp told reporters in Belgrade on Thursday evening, that the 26-year-old Nmecha had assured him that he meant no harm by his actions.

"Last weekend I ​saw Felix score two great goals and saw the celebration and then the gesture. I thought nothing of it at the time, but then it all kicked off," he said.

"As the controversy escalated, I started looking into the details of the subject and trying to form a clear picture of it.

"I confronted him with all the things you (reporters) might have confronted him with. He told me that it had nothing to do with that at all, and that he loves all people and does not discriminate against anyone."

He then said that Nmecha had agreed not to repeat the celebration.

In Friday's match, Klopp's goal will be to keep alive Germany's chances of reaching the Nations League quarterfinals with a win over Serbia. Germany are third in Group A2 with 5 points, trailing the Netherlands and Greece, who both have 8. Serbia, who Germany beat 2-0 in Munich last month, are still without a win.

"We feel well prepared," Klopp said, adding that his team were committed to earning "a final" for the last group last group game on Monday in Berlin against the Netherlands.

Klopp also expressed his disappointment that only a few thousand Serbian children would be admitted to the stadium due to a spectator ban. Originally, the game was to be played behind closed doors after Serbia was sanctioned for racist and discriminatory behavior by its fans. However, a clause in the UEFA rules allows a selected group of guests to attend. Now children under 15 accompanied by teachers or football coaches are expected to be at the match.

"We're expecting some 5,000 guests," a spokesman for the Serbian FA told the DPA news agency. The stadium's capacity is 55,000. The German FA has been allocated just 50 tickets for its fans.

#945. Ice hockey impasse as Russia threatens sanctions on Canada, Germany

Two weeks after the CAS ordered ice hockey's governing body to reintegrate Russia into international play, a solution remains elusive. Now Russia has threatened to take legal action against two tournament hosts.

"Should Canada and Germany refuse to allow the Russian team to participate, we will demand compensation, enforce the postponement of the competitions, and impose sanctions on the organizers," Russian Ice Hockey Federation President Vladislav Tretiak told the TASS news agency.

"There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed," Tretiak said after a presidential sports council meeting in Moscow on Thursday.

"The IIHF as a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, don't hold it at all, or impose sanctions on Canada."

The threat comes after the Canadian government confirmed Wednesday that it would not allow Russian players to take part in the IIHF World Junior Championship starting on December 26 in Alberta.

"Canada's position is unequivocal: as long as Russia continues ⁠its war of aggression ​against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual," Adam van Koeverden, Canada's secretary of sport, said in a statement on Wednesday. "Canada will continue to stand with Ukraine."

Following the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruling in late October, in which it said the security concerns the IIHF cited for barring Russian teams from taking part in international tournaments was not sufficient, the world governing body pledged to work to comply with the decision.

On November 8, Norway said it had been bumped from the World Juniors tournament and had been informed by the IIHF that Russia would take its place. Several other national hockey associations said they had received a revised schedule for the tournament and stated they would not play against Russia. The IIHF has not confirmed the change.

Germany has been watching developments related to the World Juniors and host nation Canada closely, as it is set to host the IIHF World Championship in Gelsenkirchen, Mannheim and Düsseldorf starting on May 14.

With several nations saying they will not play Russia and major sponsors threatening to pull out, a German government spokesman described the prospect of hosting the tournament under these conditions as "effectively impossible."

However, Germany has ruled out taking the Canadian approach.

Ronald Rauhe, Germany's minister of state for sport, said Wednesday that refusing to grant visas was "not a solution for the [German] ice hockey federation [DEB], nor is it a solution for successfully hosting a world championship anywhere."

At the same time, though, he expressed support for the DEB in its wish to host the tournament as planned.

"We believe that we should channel all our energy and efforts into helping sport — and ice hockey in particular — find a solution, which would, of course, entail excluding Russia from the World Championship."

What makes things even more complicated for German officials are concerns that taking a hard-line on Russia could jeopardize Munich's chances as it bids to host the Summer Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044.

The International Olympic Committee (IOC) recently lifted its sanctions on Russian athletes and suspension of the Russian National Olympic Committee, opening the door for their return to competition despite the ongoing war in Ukraine.

The thinking goes that the IOC would expect national Olympic committees bidding to host an Olympic Games to follow its lead. The IOC is set to decide in the next few weeks whether Munich advances to the next stage of the process.

For now, though, the ball appears to be in the IIHF's court, after Ottawa confirmed its refusal to grant Russians visas to play in the World Juniors. How the dispute regarding that tournament gets resolved could go a long way to finding a solution for the men's tournament in Germany in May.
