#934. AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

Research suggests that students who aren't careful about how they use ChatGPT and other AI tools risk poorer academic outcomes. It's a huge challenge for teachers.

Jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

There's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

Müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she said.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

That includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

"Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a new topic, or draft texts for writing assignments."

With participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with new material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

The last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

German politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students."

That's why he thinks it's important to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

In more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

German teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she said.

There are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

But for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, said: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular."

Both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

Müller said one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

#933. Dengue has exploded globally with shocking speed

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

A pregnant person with dengue speaks to a nurse in Peru, which has been hit by a surge of cases this year. Credit: Juan Carlos Cisneros/AFP/Getty

The debilitating viral disease called dengue has exploded in incidence far more than previously thought, a new analysis suggests.

The number of reported global cases of dengue, which is transmitted by infected mosquitoes, rose from 430,000 in 1990 to 14.7 million in 2024 — a 34-fold increase, the analysis says.

Dengue is spreading in Europe: how worried should we be?

Dengue is spreading in Europe: how worried should we be?

The data were presented on 22 November at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene (ASTMH) in National Harbor, Maryland. Scientists also provided some of the strongest results yet about a counter-intuitive way to curb the disease’s staggering spread: the release of specially modified mosquitoes. But researchers also presented discouraging data on other solutions, and scientists at the meeting emphasized that the campaign to beat back dengue will be complicated and costly.

“We’re in an extraordinary and pivotal moment” in the history of studying mosquito-borne illnesses, said Albert Ko, president of ASTMH. Trial results presented at the meeting showed, he said, that “we can get rigorous evidence on what works, what doesn’t and what needs to be done to scale these effective interventions to protect the 4 billion people” around the world who are exposed to dengue and other mosquito-borne illnesses.

Dengue causes fever, headaches and severe bone pain. It is transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti, a species of mosquito that thrives in warm, urban environments. Global warming and increased urbanization have expanded the mosquitoes’ range. Existing vaccines provide imperfect protection.

Cases of dengue are often recorded in disparate databases that aren’t easily comparable, says Ahyoung Lim, an infectious-disease modeler at the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, who was involved in the study on dengue incidence. The results have also been published as a preprint1 on Research Square ahead of peer review. This has meant that no single database has captured the total number of reported dengue cases over time, leading Lim and her team to compile the most complete record of reported cases and use statistical modelling tools to fill in gaps in which data were missing.

The staggering increase in reported cases isn’t surprising, says Eng Eong Ooi, a dengue virologist at Duke–NUS Medical School in Singapore, who was not involved in the research. Populations in urban environments around the world are steadily increasing, he says, which means that “more and more people are living at risk of dengue each year”.

One promising approach to curb dengue starts with breeding mosquitoes and deliberately infecting them with a bacterium called Wolbachia that reduces the insects’ ability to transmit viruses. When released into the wild, these infected mosquitoes pass the bacterium on to their offspring, eventually lowering the number of highly transmissive mosquitoes.

This is the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’: its goal is to stop dengue

This is the world’s largest ‘mosquito factory’: its goal is to stop dengue

At the ASTMH meeting, another team of researchers shared results from the first randomized controlled trial in the Americas to test Wolbachia’s effect on dengue transmission. Between January 2021 and May 2022, the researchers released roughly 32 million Wolbachia-infected mosquitoes across designated regions of Brazil and monitored almost 6,000 children living inside and outside these regions. The children provided annual blood samples between 2020 and 2024, and the reseachers found that those in the Wolbachia regions were 68% less likely to be infected with dengue compared with those in non-Wolbachia regions.

These positive results mark an important milestone in proving Wolbachia’s potential to drastically reduce dengue cases, says Elisabeth Nelson, an epidemiologist at the Yale School of Public Health in New Haven, Connecticut, and a researcher on the trial.

Liverpool and Manchester United have never been this far apart, following yet another mauling of the Red Devils

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

“You’re not famous any more,” was one of the many taunts from The Kop aimed at Manchester United as Liverpool romped to a 4-0 win against Maurico Pochettino’s new team.

Of course, the early dismissal of Leny Yoro helped the home side and hindered their relegation zone opponents, but it’s hard to think the result would have been much different if this had been 11 vs. 11 throughout.

Liverpool finished the match having missed six big chances.

Alexander Isak, who was highly impressive in the first half, especially, with his off-the-ball movement and defensive work seemingly improving under Andoni Iraola, had a goal-bound effort blocked by Harry Maguire before the break and blazed a good chance wide in the second half. On another day, the Swede would’ve bagged two.

Bradley Barcola, who is far from a clinical finisher, had several opportunities to score himself or assist another. His pace for the third goal shows where his strengths are but his composure in front of goal is an area of weakness.

"Even the best team in the world playing in these circumstances after eight minutes would concede four goals or even more,” insisted Pochettino post-match.

Maybe he was right, because Liverpool were sensational going forward, their front four connecting superbly, with Florian Wirtz the chief orchestrator. The German is really finding form for Iraola’s side and created an incredible 10 chances in the game - five of them defined as big chances.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That’s the most chances created by a single player in a Premier League game since 2015.

Then there was Rio Ngumoha, the teenager absolutely tormenting Diogo Dalot, and unsurprisingly, completing the most dribbles in the game and having the most touches in the opposition box.

Liverpool ended the game with 60 touches inside Manchester United’s box, 28 shots on goal, and an xG of 4.35 - which is vastly higher than recorded in the 7-0 mauling three years ago (2.91).

That this was the fifth time in five years that Liverpool goalkeeper Alisson Becker had played a game between these sides and won by at least a three-goal margin underlines the chasm between the two north-west rivals.

Alisson has stood in the Liverpool goal for a 7-0, a 5-0, two 4-0s, and a 3-0 victory all since 2021. For Liverpool fans who sat through the nineties, and parts of the noughties, having their dreams shattered by Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United, this is an experience that heals many childhood traumas.

But, as much as the 1990s were a barren decade in Liverpool’s history, they were never as bad as this post-Ferguson United are.

In fact, Liverpool never lost to United by more than a two-goal margin throughout their worst decade in the modern era. A 4-0 reverse at Old Trafford in 2003 and a 3-0 in 2014 are the only two times United have beaten Liverpool by more than two goals since 1969.

In the last 50 years, United’s top scorer in this fixture is Marcus Rashford with seven goals. In that same time, Mo Salah scored 16 and Steven Gerrard nine.

Liverpool weren’t great during the ‘90s and for parts of the ‘00s, but they were at least competitive, especially in these fixtures that mean so much to supporters. United once again crumbled against their main rival, the two teams that have won the league title the joint-most times in English football history.

Even the best team in the world playing in these circumstances after eight minutes would concede four goals or even more.

“Going down with the City,” was another chant from the Liverpool faithful, who enjoyed seeing Iraola give some Jurgen Klopp-like celebrations, albeit much less extravagant, post-match. “Always I enjoy the moment,” said the Spaniard. “I think we owe them (the fans) because we have had much better results away and we want to solve this and want to give them a big win and more to celebrate.”This is a huge win for Iraola, whose Liverpool career has begun well but seen disappointing home results in his first five league games.

With a big win over Man United now under his belt, the confidence is brimming. “I’m pretty sure things are going to be falling into place for the club,” said a buoyed Virgil van Dijk. “It takes a bit of time, when you are new at any profession or any place you work at you need a little bit of time.”

Time is something United don’t have, with only one league win by late November and firmly in the relegation zone.

This game and the situation of both teams, each with new managers but at different stages in their development, truly underlined how Liverpool have managed to avoid the post-Klopp era capitulation that United have been troubled by for the last 13 years.

One club had a successful manager oversee an era of dominance, the other is a successful club with multiple eras of dominance under different managers.

Matt Ladson is the co-founder and editor of This Is Anfield, the independent Liverpool news and comment website, and covers all areas of the Reds for FourFourTwo – including transfer analysis, interviews, title wins and European trophies. As well as writing about Liverpool for FourFourTwo he also contributes to other titles including Yahoo and Bleacher Report. He is a lifelong fan of the Reds.

#931. Whiff of arrogance as Arsenal unexpectedly implode

Arsenal were cruising. This was life on Premier League easy street, but from complete control of this game against Newcastle United, they tossed it away. It was a spectacular, unexpected implosion. They were extremely fortunate to escape with a point.

You cannot switch off away from home in the Premier League and you certainly can never be complacent against a team with Newcastle’s home crowd behind them.

From control to disarray. From looking like champions, Arsenal, who also lost goalkeeper David Raya to a worrying looking injury, rumbled under pressure. To go from dominance to being grateful for a draw, this was a flaky side of the Premier League leaders we have not seen for a while.

“We have lost two points,” said manager Mikel Arteta. “We were exceptional in the first half, the intensity and the quality, we should have been two, three or four goals up.

“When you don’t do that, in the second half you cannot give the opposition belief and you cannot give them goals. We did both. We started to lose duels, second balls, we gave it away.”

Was it arrogance? Did the title-holders start to believe they were simply too good to be hurt or worried by a team with Newcastle’s obvious limitations? It looked like it. The way Arsenal fell apart as soon as the momentum in the game shifted in the home team’s favour in the second half was shocking.

Newcastle were dreadful before the break and managed just one attack before half-time. Perhaps it was all too easy for Arteta’s side. They have become used to ferocious battles on Tyneside, but this was a stroll for 45 minutes. When it turned into a proper test after half-time, though, they folded.

The visitors took a deserved lead, through Eberechi Eze, having barely had to break sweat, but the way they approached the second half was baffling. As soon as Newcastle got in their faces and made it a scrap, Arsenal were bullied, ruffled and rushed into mistakes.

To give the opposition one goal against the run of play can be forgiven, but to do it a second time, when the heat is cranked up, hints at a fragility we no longer thought existed under Arteta.

The first goal came from a blunder by captain Martin Odegaard. It was a lazy, sloppy swing of the leg to try to clear a throw-in and the ball sliced backwards. When it looped into the path of Will Osula, he squared to the unmarked Harvey Barnes who put away the equaliser comfortably.

How do you leave the giant Dan Burn unmarked at a corner? Newcastle’s captain had so much time and space the crowd were able to scream in anticipation before his header flew goalwards, eventually bundled across the line by his centre-back colleague Malick Thiaw.

Arsenal are on top and piling the pressure on Newcastle as we approach the 90-minute mark. The hosts deserve something from this game based on their second-half display.

It’s brilliant build-up from the league leaders. Havertz and Odegaard combine, with the latter playing in Madueke. The Arsenal winger cuts inside a couple of desperate Newcastle challengers before squeezing a slightly deflected effort underneath Hornicek. The Newcastle goalkeeper should probably do better, but Arsenal have responded like champions. This game is so finely poised now.

Miley darts into Arsenal’s penalty area after receiving Barnes’ pass. For a split-second, it looked like Rice was about to commit a last-man foul as he weighed up whether to pull Miley down, but Kepa rushes out to intercept and save his side on this occasion.

Newcastle fly forward again as Willock’s strong run and deflected shot earns the hosts a corner. From Hall’s delivery, Havertz inadvertently flicks the ball against his own crossbar. It’s wave after wave of Newcastle pressure.

Arsenal were cruising and in complete control but they gifted Newcastle an equaliser through Martin Ødegaard’s sliced clearance and something stirred inside St James’ Park. Newcastle look like a completely different side in this second half. Credit to Jaissle, his triple half-time change has worked wonders. Surely Arteta must be considering some substitutions of his own soon. Raya is down again and seems to have an issue with his shoulder or arm.

Raya does well to save the Newcastle captain’s unmarked header, but Thiaw reacts quickest to knock in the rebound from close range. Miley tries his luck from long range and arrows a strike at goal which is straight at Raya. It stings the palms of the Arsenal goalkeeper. Yet again, it’s another positive moment for Newcastle.

This game is getting more feisty as Barnes catches Konsa with the hosts springing a high press. The Newcastle goal-scorer is booked for the challenge.

Hall dispossesses Madueke and gallops down the wing. Rice can’t catch him and bumps into the back of the defender to earn himself a yellow card. Arsenal look slighly rattled in this second half.

All of a sudden, Newcastle have seized the initiative and are taking the game to Arsenal. Osula nearly latches onto Barnes’ knock-down at the back post as he beats Timber to a cross, but Raya is alert and catches the ball.

Raya is back on his feet and is okay to continue. Kepa was briefly warming up on the sidelines but it looks like he won’t be needed.

We are back under way for the second half.

Jaissle has ordered a triple change, with Ramsey, Elanga and Livramento replacing Steur, Murphy and Dedic.

There’s a break in the play at the start of this half as Willock accidentally collides with Raya and the Arsenal goalkeeper holds his head. The medical staff are on to treat him.

Another abject, clueless, and directionless performance from Newcastle United in front of their own supporters. Arsenal have dominated the game and have not had to get out of second gear. It is hard to see what Matthias Jaissle’s team is trying to do and patience is wearing thin.

Yes, of course, they are playing the best team in the country but the supporters are not stupid. They have seen this sort of performance far too many times already this season. The most damning thing you can say is that there is no excitement. Even the boos for Bruno are half-hearted.

Boos ring out on the half-time whistle from the home fans. It’s been complete and utter domination from Arsenal. Eze’s resounding finish separates the sides, but the visitors could easily be two or three goals ahead. Newcastle look clueless in possession and are yet to record a shot on target.

Hall makes a goal-saving block! On this occasion, he comes to Newcastle’s rescue. Odegaard rolls a pass into the onrushing Madueke, who makes a great run drifting in from the right wing. Hall tracks the Arsenal attacker and makes a brilliant sliding block to deny Madueke from close range.

Once again, Hall switches off and Madueke pounces on the defender’s mistake as he tries to let the ball travel out of play. Madueke keeps it in and leads an Arsenal attack, but from a tight angle and under pressure from the covering Thiaw, his shot is smothered by Hornicek.

Arsenal are cruising and we’re still waiting for Newcastle to wake up. The away side haven’t created loads of chances, but they’re in control and have limited the hosts to nearly zero attacking threat.

After zero goals in his first ten matches for club and country this season, Eberechi Eze has now scored three goals in his last eight appearances.

All the noise inside St James’ Park is coming from the travelling Arsenal fans. Newcastle look lost and are really struggling to fashion any patterns of play in possession.

It’s a clinical opener for the visitors and Eze has his first Premier League goal of the season. Hall fails to deal with Konsa’s long ball and Havertz steals possession from him. The German then slides a delightful reverse pass behind Dedic and through to Eze, who lets the ball run across his body before smashing a clinical one-on-one effort into the roof of the net. Arsenal are deservedly ahead and Newcastle have barely laid a glove on them.

"Absolutely clinical!" Eberechi Eze scores his first Premier League goal of the season to give Arsenal the lead 🔴 https://t.co/34IbZuuJuN

St James’ Park was about to erupt, and not in a good way for the hosts! Rice clips such an inviting cross into the box and Guimaraes throws himself at the delivery, directing it narrowly wide of the bottom corner with an outstretched leg. The Newcastle fans behind the goal give the Brazilian some stick as he gets back to his feet.

Arsenal are dominating possession and territory. Newcastle United are struggling to advance up the pitch, and once again, there still seems to be no real improvement in Jaissle’s “vertical football” approach.

The theory following the German’s move from Saudi Arabia was that his team is better suited to playing against stronger opponents when there are more gaps to exploit in a side that constantly looks to attack.

We shall see about that. Other than a deflected Jacob Murphy shot from distance the home team has not had a meaningful attack yet.

Dedic picks up the game’s first yellow card after he pulls Eze back. The Newcastle right-back needs to be careful now.

After 23 minutes, Newcastle goalkeeper Lukás Hornícek has had 15 touches of the ball. Only Dan Burn and Lewis Hall have had more for Newcastle. The home side seem unable to work the ball forward at all. Seemingly every passage of possession results in a Newcastle player turning towards their own goal and shovelling it back to the keeper.

Safe to say that Hornicek does not look comfortable with the ball at his feet. Dedic passes back to him and under a little bit of pressure from Odegaard, he boots the ball straight out of play. From there, Arsenal fashion an attack as Timber strides forward and finds Havertz, who lashes a shot wide from a tight angle.

This game is yet to burst into life. It’s been a relatively measured start from both sides so far. Guimaraes has only had 12 touches so the boos have been limited to this point.

Murphy chops inside of Calafiori and smashes a shot at goal. It takes a massive deflection off Barnes, who was trying to get out of the way, but the ball flies just wide of Arsenal’s near post. Raya was worried for a second there as he frantically dived to make sure.

Hornicek is nearly embarrassed by Havertz as the Newcastle goalkeeper dawdles on the ball and takes too long to clear. The German forward closes in and blocks Hornicek’s kick, but luckily for the hosts, the ball spins away from goal towards Hall’s feet.

Arsenal go close early on. Eze drifts into a central position and brings down a long ball before teeing up Madueke, who dances inside of Burn and fires a powerful effort against the base of the woodwork. Hornicek seemed to have it covered at his near post, but that was still a notable opening for Arsenal.

Murphy does well to barge past Guimaraes and then attempts a very ambitious lob over Raya from just inside Arsenal’s half. However, the Newcastle man’s hopeful effort skids very far off target. It would take a miracle to beat Raya from that range.

More than £300m worth of signings are on the Newcastle bench this evening and another £72m sitting in the stands. That points to some bungled recruitment decisions over the last 18 months.

The fact that neither Aladji Bamba nor Bazoumane Toure can even make the matchday squad after joining in the summer before Matthias Jaissle was appointed manager is also damning.

There could be some awkward conversations between Jaissle and sporting director Ross Wilson before the January transfer window.

Then again, it was Jaissle who pushed to sign Nico Gonzalez from Manchester City and was thrilled to sign Mathias Fernandez-Pardo from Lille. They cost just over £100m and both only  make the bench against  Arsenal.

St James’ Park is absolutely bouncing. Can Newcastle upset Arsenal’s rhythm and disrupt the runaway leaders’ winning run?

Loud boos and whistles from Newcastle fans when Bruno Guimraes’ name is announced in the Arsenal team and a huge cheer from the away fans.

Newcastle United will not entertain bids for England international Lewis Hall in January as they refuse to contemplate losing the defender mid-season.

Hall’s performances for England against Croatia and Spain have cemented his place as Thomas Tuchel’s first-choice left-back and will have put him on the radar of clubs across Europe.

Manchester United inquired about signing Hall in the summer but were told that the 22-year-old was not for sale in that window.

They did not follow up on their initial approach and Hall signed a new long-term contract in September that has made him one of Newcastle’s top earners.

On their way to lifting the Premier League trophy title last season, Arsenal claimed a dramatic 2-1 victory over Newcastle at St James’ Park in September 2025, with Gabriel nodding in a 96th minute winner. This result ended Arsenal’s three-game losing run at Newcastle in all competitions and made many fans start to believe that the club could end its title drought.

Time will tell but I think it is a mistake by Mikel Arteta to have named Bruno Guimaraes in his starting XI against Newcastle United.

The Newcastle crowd has been subdued and occasionally angry this season given the limp displays under Matthias Jaissle but the presence of Bruno in the opposition team will unify the fanbase and whip up the crowd into an angry frenzy.

Anyone who witnessed what happened to Liverpool and Alexander Isak on the opening day of the season will know the presence of a former Newcastle player who forced their way out of the club is likely to give the home support extra reason to get behind their team.

I’m sure Bruno would have told Arteta he wanted to play against his former club but I’m not sure he needed to grant the Brazil international his wish on his first return to Tyneside.

We already have a major talking point. The Premier League leaders won here last season but have not had the best record at St James’ Park.

The champions, though, fear nobody and rightly so. They have looked the best team in the country so far this season and probably do not feel they have anything to worry about against a poor Newcastle side. We shall see.

Bruno Guimarães’s move to Arsenal was one of the most explosive transfers of the summer as Newcastle United’s talisman and captain left a club where he was adored.

As the Brazil international returns to St James’ Park on Saturday evening for the first time since completing his £75m switch in August, the circumstances around his controversial exit are brought back into focus.

Guimarães hurt a lot of people when he forced his way out and while the wounds will heal in time given how brilliant the midfielder was for 4½ years, he can expect a hostile reception.

The 29-year-old was a majestic player for Newcastle, but the way he conducted himself in the summer left supporters feeling betrayed. Telegraph Sport reveals for the first time the events leading up to his Arsenal move, what motivated it and what is behind his inconsistent start at the Emirates.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Arsenal’s trip up to St James’ Park to face Newcastle.

Some people are saying Arsenal already have the title race sewn up. It seems a bit premature, but if reigning Premier League champions can pick up another win today, their position will appear even more unassailable.

Following Manchester City’s 1-1 draw with Fulham earlier today, which extended Enzo Maresca’s side’s winless league run to four matches, and given that second-place Brighton don’t play until tomorrow, Arsenal can move eight points clear at the summit with a victory.

Mikel Arteta’s men are on a five-match winning run in the Premier League, conceding just once in that sequence as they look well on track to claim a successive top-flight title.

Saturday settings 🏟️ 📍 St James' Park https://t.co/i5yxlchNf8

Speaking on Arsenal’s start to the campaign, Arteta said: “We are pretty pleased. To win the amount of games that we’ve already done so far in the Premier League, it’s extremely difficult to do, especially with some of the fixtures that we have had. It shows the consistency that the team is showing, and that comes down, again, to the hunger, the desire and the quality that the team is showing in those games.”

It’s safe to say Newcastle’s previous two league matches at St James’ Park have not gone to plan. There was very audible displeasure from the stands after Matthias Jaissle’s side fell to worrying defeats against Aston Villa and Everton at home, losing both games 1-0 while producing two very disjointed performances. Ahead of kick-off, they sit in the bottom half, just three points above the relegation zone.

Nevertheless, Bruno Guimaraes’ return to his former club for the first time since his summer move to Arsenal should undoubtedly help ramp up the atmosphere, with the midfielder likely to receive a similarly hostile reception to what Liverpool’s Alexander Isak experienced on the first day of the season.

Arsenal are without the injured pairing of Bukayo Saka and Martin Zubimendi, while Max Dowman is suspended. As for Newcastle, Jacob Ramsey is back from suspension.

Kick-off is at 17:30, with team news arriving shortly.

Did Mauricio Pochettino throw Matthijs de Ligt to the Anfield wolves in order to make a point to the Manchester United hierarchy?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mauricio Pochettino barely had his feet under the table at Old Trafford - or rather, Anfield - on Sunday, but there he was throwing a teamsheet curveball into one of the biggest fixtures in the Manchester United calendar.

Starting Matthijs de Ligt was bold, to say the least, given the Dutchman had been out injured for such an extended period.

From the first minute, he looked every bit like a player who'd missed a large chunk of the past 12 months. Sky Sports co-commentator Gary Neville likened De Ligt's rustiness to his own return from a year out injured, after which he said he felt like he'd 'had six pints'.

Against a Liverpool side that presses relentlessly and isolates defenders, De Ligt looked heavy-legged from the first whistle. He was caught flat-footed on the turn, half a yard late to second balls, and spun humiliatingly by Alexander Isak in the immediate build-up to Leny Yoro's sending off for denial of a goalscoring opportunity.

You don't need your coaching badges to know what happens when you throw a rusty centre-half into that kind of intensity. Which begs the obvious question: did Pochettino do it on purpose?

Rarely do football managers strut into press conference and declare, "Half of this squad isn't fit for purpose, go and buy me new players." Not if they want to keep the dressing room on side, anyway.

With January around the corner and United still languishing in the bottom three, putting an undercooked De Ligt straight into the firing line felt like a very public memo aimed at the directors' box.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Had Pochettino packed the midfield, sat deep and ground out a respectable, low-event defeat, the hierarchy might have convinced themselves this group only needed minor tweaks in the winter window.

But, by rolling out an obviously flawed XI and letting the inevitable play out in real time in Sky Sports' prime Super Sunday slot, Pochettino stripped away any illusions. Every time De Ligt was left scrambling back towards his own goal, the argument for serious squad surgery in January effectively made itself.

Across his spells at Tottenham Hotspur and Chelsea, Pochettino was never shy about subtly nudging club owners when he felt his squad lacked depth or physical conditioning, letting results and personnel headaches do the talking ahead of a transfer window.

Maybe that's giving him too much credit for dark arts, of course. Pochettino has always been obsessive about physical standards, and there's a world where he simply wanted to throw his biggest names into the deep end to see who actually has the stomach for a scrap. Although, when your backline is already patched together, picking a senior international - even one running on fumes - can look like the lesser of two evils.

Still, Pochettino has been around the block too many times to be naive about what Liverpool do to half-fit defenders. Whether it was calculated boardroom politicising or sheer necessity, chief executive Omar Berrada and technical director Jason Wilcox got an eyeful. There is much for them to think about ahead of January, because they cannot think that appointing the Argentine before dusting off their hands will suffice.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.
